top_reviews.content:
The de Young is a standout among Bay Area museums, offering a thoughtfully curated collection even during renovations. Despite the collection not being exhaustive on our visit, it remains a highlight for anyone seeking a memorable museum experience.

Its wonderful design, including a striking observation deck, and strong emphasis on non-European collections, make the de Young unique. The Indigenous and Papua New Guinean displays in particular exemplify the museum’s commitment to diversity and artistic depth.

Special exhibits add extra value, though the museum’s core collection is the main draw. During our visits to the Monet and Anime exhibits, it was a pleasant bonus that special exhibit tickets also included general admission. Admission is also free for Bay Area residents, making the experience even more accessible.

While the outdoor dining area is beautiful, I recommend eating elsewhere due to the high cost of refreshments, such as nearly $10 for a bottle of water. That said, it is well worth a day trip if you can swing it and are in the area!

Went for the Monet and Venice exhibit. Wow. I'm glad we visited on a timed one because it got full rather quickly. The paintings were lovely. There were even paintings from other painter's of Venice. The colors were different from photos, some are brighter with awesome texture. The reflections do not show also on photos, you almost miss it at first glance and then you notice the reflection with awe. The rest of the museum is fun to see as well including the gift shop. Service is nice and efficient.

The de Young Museum is one of our favorite places to bring the kids because it strikes the perfect balance between exhibitions, and family‑friendly spaces. We spent a few hours exploring and still felt like there was more to see.

The museum’s American Art collection includes works tied to well‑known artists like O’Keeffe, Kahlo, Rivera, and Asawa, and the galleries are arranged in a way that makes it easy to move at your own pace. The kids loved the big sculptures and anything with bright colors, and we appreciated the mix of contemporary and traditional pieces.

The African and Oceanic art galleries were a big hit — the masks, textiles, and carved figures are visually striking and easy for kids to connect with. We also enjoyed the photography rooms, especially the Ansel Adams landscapes, which offered a quiet moment in the middle of our visit.

The Hamón Observation Tower is a must‑see. It’s free, and the views of Golden Gate Park and the city are incredible. The kids treated it like a lookout tower and tried to spot every landmark they could.

Overall, the de Young is a great choice for families. It’s spacious, peaceful, and full of art that sparks conversation. We left feeling inspired and already planning our next visit.

Located in Golden Gate Park, the de Young Museum is a gem. Collections include First Nation, Pacific Islander, Middle East, European and American. Paintings, furniture, ceramic, glass, textiles, and an extensive tapestry collection. Visit the observation deck on the top floor which is free with admission. Week I attended was the annual  festival pairing floral displays with art. Easy to get to from downtown and there is a cafe. I would first go to the San Francisco Botanical Garden, a 5 minute walk from Museum in the morning and then de Young in afternoon.

What a beautiful day, took my adult son to see the Egyptian exhibit "Treasures of the Pharaohs" which runs through January 2027. Easy to get there and parking is available at the Music Concourse Garage for ~$10. I got out tickets in advance $40 each. Also got to go in other areas including an exhibit from 1700-1800s Oceania (Papau New Guinea). It was spooky but the craftsmanship of the items on display was awe inspiring. Then strolled through GG Park, food trucks and benches and gardens are at every turn and restaurants and shops are plentiful around the major exits of the park. I highly recommend the Egyptian exhibit. There's a fountain/pool of lotus behind the building in GG Park which was lovely to see.

top_reviews.content:
One of the absolute highlights of our San Francisco trip was visiting Musée Mécanique. If you’ve never been, you’re missing one of the city’s true hidden gems.

Walking through the museum is like stepping back in time. It’s filled with beautifully restored antique, coin-operated arcade games, fortune tellers, mechanical displays, and vintage amusements—many of them still fully functional after decades, and in some cases, more than a century.

What made our visit even more special was meeting the son of the owner. He was incredibly welcoming and generous with his time, taking us behind the scenes to show us how several of these incredible machines work. Seeing the inner mechanics and hearing the stories behind these historic pieces gave us an even greater appreciation for the craftsmanship that went into creating them.

I’ve visited quite a few antique arcades over the years, but this collection is easily one of the finest I’ve ever seen. It’s not just an arcade—it’s a living museum where history comes alive one coin at a time.

Whether you’re a history buff, an arcade enthusiast, or just looking for something unique to do in San Francisco, I can’t recommend Musée Mécanique enough. It’s a fascinating experience for all ages and a place I’ll definitely be visiting again.

🎮⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

The space was clean, spacious, and well kept. Change machines were readily available throughout the building, and the staff were friendly and attentive when a machine needed assistance. It is a very cool piece of history and a great place to sit or wander around for an hour. Overall, I think it is an excellent location and well worth stopping by.

I bought the Gardens of Golden Gate Park pass—three gardens for three days for $25—which was a much better value for me than paying $15 to visit just the Botanical Garden for one day. I also visited the Japanese Tea Garden, which is $16 for a one-day ticket.

If you only have an hour or less, the Japanese Tea Garden is a good choice. But if you have several hours and want to wander among beautiful examples of flowers and plants from around the world in a more peaceful environment, I much preferred the San Francisco Botanical Garden.

The San Francisco Botanical Garden was a highlight of my trip to San Francisco and the best botanical garden I have ever visited. If you're an introvert or simply looking for some peace and quiet amid the bustle of San Francisco, this 55-acre garden with more than 8,000 different kinds of plants provides a wonderful escape.

What I especially loved was that you aren't limited to the main pathways connecting the different garden areas. Within many of the gardens are smaller, winding dirt and pebble paths that let you wander right alongside the plants and beneath the trees. You can really immerse yourself in the surroundings and get in some serious forest-bathing rest and relaxation.

Some of my favorite areas were the Moon Viewing Garden, Ancient Plant Garden, Australia Garden, Andean Cloud Forest, Southeast Asian Cloud Forest, Fragrance Garden, and Redwood Grove. Each felt different enough that wandering from one to another was almost like traveling through different parts of the world without leaving Golden Gate Park.

One practical tip: Take a picture of the large garden map when you arrive so you'll have it on your phone. With 55 acres and all those little winding paths, it's surprisingly easy to lose your sense of direction. I found some of the exit signs confusing and occasionally felt as though they were sending me back and forth when I was trying to find my way out.

Give yourself time here. For me, this wasn't a garden to race through checking off sights. The pleasure was in slowing down, wandering down those little paths, getting close to the leaves and trees, and simply enjoying being surrounded by so much nature.

It is such a dream. San Francisco’s botanical gardens had so many different plant species. I was baffled at the possibility that they all could grow well there. It was a dream. It wasn’t so busy and well worth a visit.
It's a beautiful place to spend a whole day enjoying nature's at its finest,  beautiful plants,  benches,  lots of shade and grass if you want to lay down and soak up the sun.

The bakery was fairly busy, with some interior and exterior spaces occupied. Upon arrival, counter staff could not locate the pre-staged to-go bag on the holding racks. After cross-referencing email confirmation and register data, the order had to be manually fulfilled on the fly. The interaction lacked basic hospitality standards; the associate appeared visibly bothered by the packaging task, and no thank you was offered upon handoff.

From a distance, the employee was observed sharply tapping the small pastry box down on the countertop before folding the lid flaps. Upon returning to my home for the structural audit, the consequence of this handling error was clear. The cardboard box was completely undersized for the four-inch Lemon Cream Tart, which cost $11.50. The restricted cardboard perimeter compressed the product, completely fracturing the right side of the brittle pastry crust and causing the lemon curd surface to shear and crack cleanly down the center.

The Classic Butter Croissant at $6.75 and the Pain au Chocolat at $7.25 suffered a catastrophic structural slide, tightly crowded alongside multiple baked elements into a shared container. Macro-analysis of the croissant's exterior revealed a well-defined shell with caramelized lamination bands, but both pastries completely lacked the shattering, brittle crispiness required of an elite viennoiserie matrix. Applying a standard serrated knife resulted in immediate compression rather than a clean shear. Forensic cross-sections exposed the interior crumb network, revealing an under-baked, gummy, and dense core moisture trap near the base that rendered the matrix texturally non-viable. An identical structural failure was evident in the Pain au Chocolat, where a collapsed, wet internal crumb surrounded the chocolate batons, indicating severe thermal core under-development during the bake cycle.

The Morning Bun, priced at $6.50, offered a distinct operational contrast, delivering a well-developed, satisfyingly chewy texture complemented by a vibrant, clean citrus flavor profile. The Chocolate Rye Tea Cake, also $6.50, delivered a pleasant flavor profile, but the internal crumb structure was flatly heavy, and dense, completely missing the lighter, delicate aeration expected of a premium tea cake. Total spend was $38. At a premium tier pricing model—featuring one of the priciest lemon tarts in San Francisco—there is zero operational headroom for sloppy packaging logistics, front-of-house apathy, and under-baked pastry cores. Legacy brand hype cannot mask a visible slide in daily operational execution.

top_reviews.content:
The Perfect Park Day in North Beach

​TL;DR: The ultimate park to grab world-class pizza, touch grass, and soak up the sun. Located right in the heart of North Beach (Little Italy), it’s a gorgeous, lively spot for picnics, dog-watching, and pure SF culture. Parking is tough, but the vibes are immaculate.

​🍕 The Ultimate "Grab & Go" Picnic Spot
​Washington Square is practically a front yard for some of the best food in San Francisco. Because it's nestled right in Little Italy, the move here is to grab takeout and have a feast on the lawn.

​The Food Scene: You are steps away from absolute legendary spots. Snag a legendary pie from Tony’s Pizza Napoletana, grab classic Italian comfort food from Original Joe’s, or pop into any of the nearby cafes for a pastry and espresso.

​The Setup: There is plenty of space on the lush green grass to spread out a blanket. It is the perfect spot to sit back with friends, crush some incredible food, and just enjoy the day.

​☀️ The Vibe & Culture

​This park is a beautiful melting pot of tourists, neighborhood locals, and different cultures. No matter what time of day you cruise by, there’s always something beautiful happening:

​Morning to Evening: In the morning, you’ll see neighbors practicing yoga or Tai Chi on the grass. By lunchtime, local workers are out soaking up the sun, and by the weekend, it transforms into a lively community hub with local festivals and pop-up markets.

​Dog & Kid Friendly: If you have a pup, bring them! It's a massive hub for local dog owners, and there’s plenty of room for kids to run around and play.

​The Backdrop: The views here are stunning, framed beautifully by the historic Saints Peter and Paul Church right across the street.

​🎒 Quick Insider Tips for Your Visit
​The Weather: Unlike the foggier sides of the city, North Beach usually gets pretty great, warm weather. It’s an awesome spot to actually catch some reliable rays.
​Getting There & Parking: Honestly, trying to park in North Beach can be a total headache and will definitely require some extra laps around the block. If you can, save yourself the stress and take Muni—tons of bus lines drop you off right by the square.

​Whether you're a local on a lunch break or a visitor wanting to feel the heartbeat of North Beach, this park is pure magic

top_reviews.content:
As a professional photographer and videographer, the Legion of Honor is honestly one of my absolute favorite spots in San Francisco to capture photos.

I have been inside and it is a beautiful place to take in some truly amazing artwork. The collection of European paintings and ancient art they have on display is incredible to see in person.

But for my work, the exterior grounds are where this location really shines. It has similar grand architectural features that everybody seems to love, but it tends to be far less busy than the Palace of Fine Arts. Utilizing the stunning pillars and the sweeping colonnades gives engagement and wedding photos such a luxurious and high end look.

Depending on the time of day, the lighting out in the courtyard can be drastically different. You can get something with really dramatic, harsh shadows playing off the stone, or you can get beautifully flat and even light for portraits.

The vantage points are also unbelievable. From the grounds, you can get incredible shots with iconic San Francisco landmarks like Sutro Tower and the Golden Gate Bridge right in the background. The stone balustrades and the round walls just complete the entire aesthetic.

I love the Legion of Honor, and I am sure it will not remain a hidden gem for long once I start sharing more of these pieces. If you visit, I hope you get a chance to take beautiful photos of the architecture itself. It is simply an amazing location to experience.

Such a pretty museum with one of the best views in the city. The building itself is modeled after the Palais de la Legion d’Honneur in Paris. It has big marble columns and a beautiful courtyard. In the center sits Rodin’s The Thinker...contemplating who took the best photo of him for Instagram. I went specifically for the Bouquets to Art exhibit, where floral designers create arrangements inspired by pieces in the museum. Very cool. A well spent afternoon.

The traveling Etruscan exhibit was great. Not very big, but very interesting and enjoyable. I wasn't impressed by most of the permanent collection. Mostly a lot of mid-level European painting. There were a few highlights such as the Rembrandt and the Rodin's, but I expected more from a major San Francisco museum.

As a longtime Legion of Honor member, I wanted to highlight a special exhibit celebrating International Women’s Day, running March 3–8.

Floral arrangements are placed throughout the galleries and feel like interpretations of the artworks around them, echoing the colors, shapes, and mood of the paintings and sculptures nearby. It creates a really interesting dialogue between the flowers and the art. At least - that’s my personal interpretation of its

Walking through the museum becomes a bit of a treasure hunt, with each room revealing another creative arrangement.

A beautiful and unique exhibit - definitely worth a visit.

An incredibly beautiful museum. The enormous exhibition halls are arranged harmoniously and spaciously. Because of the large size of each gallery, the museum never feels crowded or overwhelming. You walk around and explore, realizing there are many people there, yet no one gets in each other’s way. Everything is bright, clean, and even a little luxurious. At times, it felt like being inside a castle.

Unfortunately, we didn’t have enough time to explore the entire museum because we had a symphony orchestra performance planned afterward. Which means we will definitely come back again. Considering the size and scale of this museum, it’s worth setting aside anywhere from 2 to 6 hours for a visit.

They also have a huge café-restaurant and an indoor garden, so there are plenty of places to relax and enjoy a delicious meal in a beautiful setting. This is truly a must-visit place in San Francisco if you are a lover of ancient architecture, art, and monumental grandeur.

The first room was circus themed, which was fine with us, it had circus music playing which made it more of a mystery vibe which I liked a lot. The second room was silent and very dark, the theme was a lot more creepy, it had a wall pinned with stuffed animals, a broken down popcorn machine, and a broken down soda machine. This is when I started getting a feeling. The third room I did not like because it had a warlock/magician looking guy on the wall, and to escape that room we had to use “tarot cards” blocks and line them up in the correct order for our door to open. We are Christian and we did not appreciate that. That alone ruined my experience. To make escape room fun and appropriate for everyone there needs to be some sort of caution for the themes. For us and our beliefs, tarot and magic is not of God and I’m sure it’s something that could ruin the whole experience for other people as well. It’s offensive to our beliefs. Me and my husband enjoyed the challenge, it was fun trying to escape together. But it just offended us how they don’t give a warning about what could be in the themes. The employee that helped us the whole time was great, she was nice and even gave us extra time.

Julian was our game master and they were really good.

Some things to keep in mind:
- the rules or guidelines should be spoken at a speed that everyone can comprehend. First timers or anyone who may not have English be their first language may have difficulty following.
- Asking us afterwards repeatedly if we had any questions was a bit much. It’s a closed-ended question. Instead maybe ask an open-ended like what we enjoyed or found difficult?
- The Fair Game room was fun but the opening video doesn’t provide a story and give us a motive to get out before the time reaches zero.

Thank you!

Salesforce Park is one of the most unique and beautiful places to visit in downtown San Francisco. I was pleasantly surprised by how peaceful and green it feels despite being right in the middle of the city.

The park is built on top of the Salesforce Transit Center, and the design is really impressive. There are beautifully landscaped gardens, walking paths, trees, flowers, fountains, open spaces, and plenty of places to sit and relax. The combination of greenery and the surrounding skyscrapers makes for some great views and photo opportunities.

I particularly enjoyed just walking around and taking in the different sections of the park. It’s very well maintained and feels like a peaceful escape from the busy streets below. The architecture of the transit center itself is also impressive, and the park gives you a completely different perspective of downtown San Francisco.

It’s a great place to visit if you’re looking for somewhere to take a relaxing walk, enjoy some fresh air, have a coffee, or simply take a break while exploring the city. It’s also a great spot for visitors because it’s free and easy to access.

Definitely worth checking out if you’re in downtown San Francisco. A hidden gem in the middle of the city!

Salesforce Park is one of the most unique public spaces in San Francisco. The park is beautifully maintained, with excellent landscaping and a surprisingly peaceful atmosphere considering it sits above a busy transit center. The variety of plant life and greenery makes it feel like a true urban oasis, and it’s a great place to walk, relax, or take in views of the city.

That said, the signage could definitely be improved. While the park itself is enjoyable to explore, there isn’t always enough clear information about directions, features, or points of interest. The adjoining transit center can also be confusing to navigate, especially for first-time visitors. Better information screens and clearer transit signage would make the overall experience much smoother and less disorienting.

Overall, it’s a fantastic public space with impressive design and upkeep — it just needs clearer wayfinding and transit information to fully match the quality of the park itself.

The most beautiful big city in America that I have visited so far. The center is great, but the part along the coast is even more beautiful and interesting. The food in the restaurants is phenomenal (especially the crabs!) The ice cream is superb! And the space itself all around you is practically historical, every detail. It is mandatory to visit this beautiful city slowly and in detail several times.

If you’re into history or just love being by the water, the San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park is a spot you shouldn’t miss. It’s right in the Fisherman’s Wharf area, so super easy to get to.

First off, the historic ships are super cool. You can actually board them and see what life was like back in the day. The Balclutha, this big old sailing ship, was a favorite of mine. Then there’s the Eureka, an old-school steam ferryboat, which has such a unique vibe.

The visitor center is packed with interesting info and a great place to start your visit. Just across the way is the Maritime Museum, in this awesome art deco building. It has all sorts of exhibits about shipbuilding, navigation, and life at sea – plenty to keep you entertained and informed.

All in all, it’s a fantastic mix of history and scenic views. Definitely worth a visit next time you’re in San Francisco!

Alamo Drafthouse is honestly one of the best venues for hosting a technical conference! The experience is so much better than sitting in a traditional conference room all day. You get an absolutely gigantic movie theater screen that makes technical presentations, demos, and visuals look fantastic, so everyone can clearly see the content without straining their eyes.

The seating is another huge plus. Everyone gets a super comfortable, adjustable sofa-style theater seat, making it much easier to sit back, relax, and stay focused throughout the presentations. And the best part? You can order food and drinks directly from your phone, and everything is delivered right to your seat! No need to leave the room, stand in line, or miss an important part of a presentation just to grab something to eat.

Combining a massive screen, comfortable seating, great food, and convenient in-seat service makes the whole conference experience so much more enjoyable. It’s especially great for technical conferences where you want everyone to focus on the content while still feeling comfortable and relaxed.

Honestly, why are we still hosting conferences in traditional meeting rooms with tiny screens and uncomfortable chairs? 😂 All technical conferences should be held this way! Once you experience a conference at Alamo Drafthouse, going back to a conventional conference room feels like a downgrade! 😎

Sad to have to write this, but important to share our recent experience for the fellow broken-hearted Alamites.

We used to go here every few months for family movie night. Went a few weeks ago for The Odyssey. We won't be going back until there's a return to how things used to be pre-Sony.

TL;DR for prospective movie-goers: Very sad to say that you should skip the Alamo. Either go to your true locals like the Balboa, or to the corporates like AMC and Regal that can actually deliver.

Issues for Management:

1. New seats are dramatically less comfortable, recline less, and feel cheap. Check minus.

2. The food feels lower quality, almost Cisco-like. Their "special menu" items also seem much more soulless.  2-3 years ago, you'd have some special app, a few unique cocktails, a tailored entree or pizza. Today, it's a lemonade with blue + red syrup for spiderman.

3. I'm sure as victims of circumstance, the morale of the -remaining staff after lay-offs seems epically low. I feel for them.

4. The irony of the new cell phone ordering policy is absurd. To quote Alamo's new policy: "Putting ordering control directly in our guests’ hands allows us to move faster and more efficiently, creating a smoother, more responsive experience without added distraction." What a red herring. You've made a deal with the devil, laying off hardworking people in exchange for a poorly designed app and a worse customer experience. Stop trying to hide behind "efficiency" and a "more responsive experience" when you're putting people out of work for the sake of profiteering.

5. Have I mentioned that the app itself is also pretty poorly designed and nearly impossible to navigate? Sidenote - there is no way to transition tabs or previous orders from the bar to your seats, which felt like a con. I wouldn't usually complain about this, but when the new price for a 16 oz Coca-Cola is $7.99 and you're told "there's no way to honor refills if it's not in the app", you can't help but feel salty.

Ok, end rant.

Lake Chabot Regional Park is an absolutely beautiful place and easily one of the most peaceful outdoor spaces in the area. From the moment you arrive, it feels like a true escape from the city--quiet, expansive, and surrounded by nature.

The scenery alone is worth the visit. The lake is stunning, especially when the light hits the water, and the surrounding hills and greenery make it feel immersive and calming. It's the kind of place that instantly slows you down and helps you breathe a little deeper.

One of the biggest highlights is the sheer number of trails available. There are so many options, whether you're looking for a casual walk, a longer hike, or something more challenging. The trails are well maintained and offer a great mix of lake views, wooded areas, and open stretches.

It's also a great park because it works for so many different types of outings. You'll see hikers, runners, cyclists, families, and people just enjoying time outdoors. There's plenty of space, so it never feels overcrowded, even when it's busy.

Lake Chabot Regional Park is a true gem. The natural beauty, variety of trails, and peaceful atmosphere make it a place you'll want to return to again and again. Whether you're local or just visiting, it's absolutely worth spending time here.

It is a nice place to go hiking in the summer time because there is plenty of trees and shaded trails. We even spotted a falcon on the tree branch very close to us.

You can either park in the park (5 bucks) or street parking nearby.

I went on a Friday morning just after they opened and spent 2 hrs there! We came to San Fran for a bday trip and stayed in the marina area on Lombard. They had a bonus exhibit downstairs specifically about Disneyland for the 70th birthday which I absolutely loved! Very easy to follow along, they had listening devices to hear Walt and others speak about different things, sketches, merch, pictures beyond pictures and they had SO MUCH INFO from the family members to the businesses to the cartoon industry to Walt’s life it was just amazing I actually cried twice just feeling the happiness and nostalgia!

I have had a deep love for all things Disney and have been immersed in the stories my whole life because of my grandma ran “it’s a small world preschool” and was an avid Disney song listener and singer and my grandpa worked in Adventureland as a skipper and in the tiki room for years and would tell me stories about talking to Walt because the entrance he used was in Adventureland! I have wanted to go to this museum for YEARS so going through with my baby girl was just a dream!

Such a beautiful museum! This was the first date my husband and I went on 13 years ago on Valentine's Day! It's still amazing! The staff is incredible! Also, if you are military or a veteran you and your spouse gets in free! There were also food tricks across the street at the park! It was perfect!

If you have time to spare, Google the Skywalker Ranch offices. It's about 4 minutes away in the Presidio. You can see the Yoda fountain and visit the gift shop for Lucas Studios. It's an amazing location.

This place is full of history of Walt Disney and Disney Parks. I had such a great time walking around the gallery’s. They also have a cafe inside and a gift shop. Staff were kind and helpful and told about the gallery’s.

This museum provides the history of Walt disney. It contains a lot of personal photos as well as his early days of building Disney. It was interesting to see how his ideas progressed over the years. The museum covers 2 floors and is a wealth of information regarding early animation.

top_reviews.content:
History directly beneath the Golden Gate Bridge.

Fort Point is an impressive place to explore. The old brick fort, its corridors and rooms already make the visit worthwhile, but the location directly underneath the Golden Gate Bridge takes it to another level.

Walking through the fort feels a bit like discovering a hidden dungeon beneath one of San Francisco’s most famous landmarks. Great views, lots of history, and plenty to explore.

Free entry, impressive location, successful quest. 5/5.

Fort Point was on my list primarily to check on the nesting Pigeon Guillemots, but I ended up enjoying so much more than just the birds. The views from here are simply spectacular, with the Golden Gate Bridge towering right above you, sweeping views of San Francisco Bay, and the city skyline visible in the distance. It’s easily one of the best spots in the city for photographing the bridge from a unique perspective.

There’s ample parking, restrooms, and plenty of room to walk around while soaking in the scenery. Whether you’re a wildlife enthusiast, photographer, history buff, or simply visiting San Francisco for the first time, Fort Point is absolutely worth a stop.

I’ve shared the rest of the details, tips, and highlights in my photos and videos, so be sure to check those out. This is one place that truly combines history, incredible views, and wildlife all in one visit.

A great place to visit with free admission and amazing views of the Golden Gate Bridge. The fort has many interesting rooms to explore and a unique historical atmosphere. Definitely worth a stop for both the history and one of the best views in San Francisco.

Really interesting place to visit. There were quite a lot of people when I was there, but it never felt like a problem. You can still easily walk around, get to all the viewpoints, and see everything without much trouble.

There is a lot of interesting stuff inside the fort too, old equipment, ropes, barrels, different displays, and some really cool visual exhibits. It makes the place much more interesting than just coming for the view.

One thing I definitely recommend is finding the open window on the second floor with the view of the Golden Gate Bridge. That was probably one of my favorite spots there.

I visited Fort Point two years ago and was really impressed by this place! It’s a beautiful free attraction with amazing views of the Golden Gate Bridge. The bridge is stunning, and the waterfront scenery makes it well worth a visit. Parking can sometimes be challenging, so it’s better to arrive early in the morning or toward the evening. A wonderful spot to walk around, take photos, and enjoy the views!

top_reviews.content:
Great movie theatre with a lot of screens showing a variety of films.

The theatre we were in was large, clean, and had very comfortable fabric reclining chairs. The screen was large, sound was good, seat viewing angles are good in the upper section.

There are two large concession stands - one on each floor, offering a wide variety of snacks and beverages.

We were there on a Saturday afternoon and it wasn't very busy, which was nice. There were no lines for anything. I'd go back here.

This was my go-to theater for over a decade when I was living in Pacifica. For the last decade living in San Bruno, we’ve almost exclusively gone to the Century at Tanforan. While it’s much closer to home, the Tanforan theater is still living in the stone ages with their seats. Daly City has since done a full remodel, switching to the “luxury lounger” electric reclining chairs. Depending on the movie and show times, we’re more than willing to drive the extra distance to have those super comfy chairs!

The theater itself is pretty big, featuring 20 screens spanning across multiple levels. You enter from Junipero Serra Blvd where there’s a box office to purchase tickets on-site. They have the standard red text digital screen displaying all the movie times, and you select your seats right there at the window. If you purchased your tickets digitally, you can walk straight to the far doors where they’ll scan your tickets.
**Note that they no longer automatically print out ticket stubs if you scan a digital ticket. If you want one, you can ask, though it looks more like a receipt now than the traditional stub.

As soon as you enter, you go up a giant escalator to get to the main level. The main level has the most / biggest theaters (IMAX / XD), the snack shop, as well as the arcade. The snack shop features all the standard options you’d expect to see at a theater: popcorn, kettle corn, hotdogs, nachos, candy, soda, ICEE, plus ice cream and other frozen treats!

Up at the front, they have special drinks such as coffee (latte, cappuccino, mocha, caramel macchiato – hot or iced), chai latte, tea, caramel frappe, and hot chocolate. They advertise for pizza, though I’ve never seen them out. Maybe you have to ask?

They also have a bar! Pretty basic, but solid options: Draft beer (Blue Moon, 805, Michelob Ultra, Modelo Especial, Sierra Nevada), cans (Guiness, Stella, White Claw, Truly Strawberry Lemonade, Twisted Tea) wine (red & white), and frozen cocktails!

The arcade is decent, featuring some standard games like air hockey, Ms. Pac-man / Galaga, Aliens shoot-em-up, Super Shot basketball game, Batman and motorcycle racing, and a cool Star Wars game where you get into a little enclosed pod. They also have a good amount of claw and other prize games.

There are even more theaters on the 3rd floor, which is accessible by another large escalator, or a literal mountain of stairs. They have a smaller snack shop up there, though I haven’t seen it in use the last few visits, so I’m not sure if they ever use it anymore these days. I definitely remember times where it was not only open, but busy! Both levels have (nice & clean) bathrooms, and they’re also accessible via elevator.

If you’re driving in, there’s plenty of free parking in an attached multi-level garage. I recommend parking on the 2nd floor – you can exit the theater from the back on the main level, and it connects you directly to that level of the garage! There are also several restaurants right there, including Round Table, Westlake Coffee Shop, Cold Stone, sushi, ramen, and a giant seafood buffet that likely has both of those things and more.

I definitely recommend seeing a movie at the Century 20 Daly City – it’s clean, comfortable, the staff’s friendly, and it’s an all around good experience. Come out and support the theater!

The staff were rude and ill-mannered. They sold me a ticket for a movie that had already started—I had asked for the 11:45 PM showing. About 20 minutes into the film, they turned on the theater lights, and when I complained to the manager, he suspected I hadn't paid for a ticket to that specific movie. I was kicked out of the cinema with my girlfriend and two children. The manager and a security guard were very rude to my family. Their rudeness frightened my son; he has autism, didn't understand the situation, and started crying. It was only after I called the police—once we were already outside—that the manager offered four tickets to see a movie another day. The staff were incompetent and rude to two 6-year-old children. We were there to watch *Toy Story 5*.

The recliner seats here are comfortable, although we've noticed that some are starting to show some wear and can be a little loud when adjusting. The rows are spaced out nicely, so you don't really see the people in front of you, which means fewer distractions during the movie.

The location is really convenient, with a free parking structure nearby, and it's also walkable from Daly City BART.

No complaints overall—it's a convenient theater with comfortable seating and easy access by both car and public transportation.

We recently visited this theater to see Toy Story, and my nephew accidentally left his favorite stuffed animal behind. We called multiple times the next day, hoping it had been turned in to lost and found. We were ultimately told that it could not be found and that items left behind are often thrown away.

I understand theaters have to clean up after shows, but I was disappointed to hear that a child’s stuffed animal may have been discarded so quickly rather than held in lost and found. Items like stuffed animals are clearly personal belongings and often have significant sentimental value to children.

The staff did check for the item, which I appreciate, but the possibility that a child’s cherished toy was thrown away within a day left us feeling that the theater’s lost-and-found process could be more family-friendly.

Dolby viewing experience at the Metreon was awesome. After trying to find the best Dolby theater in the area, I can say that the experience at the Metreon was great. Parking was just to the south west (unfortunately $24 for just over 4 hours).

Watched Avatar: Fire and Ash there and it was the experience I was looking for. I believe it’s the Dolby 2.81:1 screen which is a bit wider than normal, but was great for Avatar. The high frame rate (HFR) looked great and the surround sound was loud and immersive without blowing my ears out. Colors were incredibly vibrant and the experience felt unique compared to a regular theater.

It was clean and the seats were comfortable and spacious. I wouldn’t change anything besides trying to get more central seats. Photo was taken in F13 and sound came a bit stronger from the left side at first, but eventually it became unnoticeable. Definitely would go back again if I wanted to show someone Avatar who appreciated a large, clear, vibrant, sharp, and comfortable viewing experience.

Going to the AMC Metreon was an amazing opportunity. They have the second largest 70mm IMAX screen in the US. Beocuse of this watching the Odessy was incredible. The absolute perfection in format to watch something so special in 70mm was impeccable.  The candy was expensive tho.

The experience of watching The Odyssey was awesome. The building, however, is somewhat confusing and the elevators never came so we had to use the stairs. The seats were not as most movie theaters I’ve visited, which is strange for the cost of the ticket. I was expecting more accommodations and ability to move and control my seat. Overpriced popcorn as well.

I had a horrible experience at this theater during an 8:00 p.m. showing of *The Odyssey*.

My boyfriend had purchased two valid tickets for us. Because the tickets were bought at the last minute, our seats were separate and located toward the back of the auditorium. Both tickets were stored on his phone.

During the movie, I realized that my phone was missing. I believed I had last used it at a nearby restaurant, but when we checked Find My, it appeared to be somewhere inside the theater building. Because the phone was not backed up and contained important information, I was understandably very anxious.

I left the auditorium and spoke to a security guard about the missing phone. He initially began walking me toward the staff area, but then told me he could not cross or search through the auditorium while the movie was playing. I asked whether he could help me after the movie ended, and he agreed. I returned to my seat expecting that the matter would be handled afterward.

Approximately 20 to 30 minutes later, the same security guard came directly to my seat inside the auditorium and told me I had to leave and speak with the manager because I supposedly had not paid for a ticket. I told him clearly that I did have a ticket, but he repeatedly insisted that I had not paid.

This was especially confusing because he had just told me that he could not move through the auditorium to assist with my missing phone, yet he was apparently able to enter the auditorium and remove me from the movie based on an incorrect ticket accusation.

I had to ask my boyfriend to leave the auditorium with me because the tickets were on his phone. Once we were outside, he showed the manager both valid tickets, and the issue was immediately resolved. We were allowed to return, but by that point we had missed part of the ending of a very long movie that we had paid to see.

The entire interaction was embarrassing, disruptive, and completely unnecessary. No one appeared to verify whether I had a valid ticket before approaching me in the middle of the movie and insisting that I had not paid. A simple, discreet request to see the ticket would have resolved everything within seconds.

The theater should review how security and management handle ticket verification, especially when tickets for multiple guests are stored on one person’s phone. Customers should not be publicly confronted and removed from an auditorium based on an unverified assumption.

I would appreciate an explanation and a refund or replacement passes, since the theater’s mistake caused us to miss part of the film and significantly damaged the experience.

We had a truly wonderful cinematic experience recently. The theater provided an exceptionally spacious and comfortable environment for our viewing pleasure. Every seat offered ample room, allowing for complete relaxation. Furthermore, the popcorn served was absolutely delightful and greatly enhanced the overall enjoyment. It was a truly memorable occasion for all of us.

Tilden Regional Park is a massive 2,079-acre escape in the Berkeley Hills, often referred to as the "jewel" of the East Bay Regional Park District. It is highly regarded for its diverse blend of natural wilderness, scenic views, and family-friendly recreational attractions.
* Diverse Attractions: The park features several unique landmarks, including the Tilden Park Merry-Go-Round, the steam-powered Redwood Valley Railway, and the Little Farm where visitors can feed cows and sheep.
* Outdoor Recreation: It offers over 39 miles of trails for hiking, biking, and horseback riding, along with swimming and fishing at Lake Anza.
* Botanical Interest: The Regional Parks Botanic Garden within the park is dedicated to California's native flora, showcasing plants from all corners of the state.
* Accessibility: The park is open daily from 5:00 AM to 10:00 PM and offers numerous picnic areas that can be reserved for groups.

It feels like stepping into a historic Irish gathering spot right in the middle of San Francisco.

The inside has plenty of character, with cozy booths, classic pub seating, and a spacious layout that somehow still feels intimate and welcoming. The décor and atmosphere alone make this place worth visiting, whether you’re there for drinks, dinner, or simply to take in the ambiance.

Great exhibits on 1/2/26...we really enjoyed the Oakland Museum of California. It was much more expansive and engaging than we expected and very well organized overall. Some sections are fuller than others, but nothing felt confusing or disjointed.

🏛️ Layout & Exhibits
The museum is divided into three main sections on three different levels: (1) California & Oakland history, (2) Science, and (3) Art.

The history exhibits were a highlight—walking through the decades made California and Oakland’s story feel much clearer and more connected. What stood out most is that everyone was genuinely engaged: the kids explored on their own (not just tagging along), and the adults were just as absorbed. It worked well for all of us at the same time.

👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Ages
Good for all ages, but younger kids will enjoy the science section the most. The history and art sections felt best suited for older kids (8+), which matched our experience. Walking through the decades of California/Oakland history helped everything click in a clear, connected way—great for homeschoolers or families who value contextual learning.

🎒 Bags, Food & Lockers
- No purses allowed, but jackets with pockets were fine
- No food or water bottles allowed inside
- Lockers available for belongings

♿ Accessibility
There are many stairs, but also ramps and elevators connecting all levels of the three museum sections. Wheelchairs are available. Security is present at entrances and throughout.

🚗 Parking (Important Notes)
There is an on-site parking garage, and you can pay inside or outside. Once you pay, you have about 15 minutes to exit.
⚠️ When the museum starts closing, everyone is pushed out at once, which caused a line to exit the garage—plan extra time.

⏰ Closing Time — Plan Ahead
Although it says they close at 5:00 PM, they begin closing everything around 4:45 PM. Bathrooms close, doors lock, and visitors are directed out. We didn’t even make it to the gift shop because we didn’t realize how firm this was.
‼️If anyone in your group needs the bathroom, go earlier—otherwise expect a long wait or to miss it entirely.

Overall: A really engaging, well-designed museum that works for meaningful family learning: kids and adults at the same time. Just plan your timing carefully near closing. Absolutely worth the visit.

Oakland Museum of California, Oakland

I’ve been here many times especially when my daughter was small, now I come here with my nieces and nephews. The museum displays changes often, so there’s always something new to see.

I usually love visiting the garden area especially on a beautiful sunny day! The garden area has been renovated so there’s many places to sit, relax and have a quick lunch when in the area.

The museum has three floors, so there’s plenty to see, so make sure you wear comfortable shoes! 👟

The bottom floor is the Nature Area, most kids love that area, to see and explore all the wild animals that roams in California. The “Welcome to Oakland” sign and “Oak tree” display is located on this floor. Awesome exhibit!

The second floor is where you pay for your admission, the gift shop is here, one of the main rooms changes to new event or exhibition. It’s also next to the entrance of Town Fare restaurant! Great food and great vibes! The other room is based on history of technology and revolutions. Old school car and television, the history of the Black Panther Party, the Chinese Excursion Act,  Angel Island, Paper brother and paper sister, the history of the great San Francisco fire and earthquake, the history of technology and so on. There’s even a small theater room too.

The top floor is mainly art and statues, many hidden rooms to explore.

We came on a weekday so that’s usually field trip days for kids, it wasn’t crowded either so we still got to see plenty of stuff.

I will always come back and visit! 💕

If you grew up in the east bay and you came here on school field trips this is not the same museum. It has been beautifully reimagined and updated. The price of admission is well worth it. Also have lunch at the cafe. We got the burger and chicken sandwich and this is probably the best museum food we’ve had. Most places charge a ton for mediocre food. Not the OMCA!

Our group from the NAACP Merced County Branch recently visited the Oakland Museum of California, and the experience was outstanding from start to finish.
We traveled in through the Amtrak Gold Runner partnership from Merced, and the museum staff were welcoming and accommodating to our intergenerational group, from elementary age students to seasoned community leaders. The exhibits were thoughtfully curated, engaging, and deeply reflective of California’s diverse history and cultural contributions. The storytelling throughout the galleries was powerful, interactive, and relevant.
We especially appreciated how the museum creates space for meaningful conversations around culture, identity, and community. It was not just a visit. It was an experience that sparked dialogue and connection long after we left.
One suggestion for improvement would be a more streamlined check in process for larger pre registered groups. An expedited line for partner programs would make arrival smoother.
Overall, an exceptional experience. We will absolutely be back, and we are already talking about the next trip.

Had an unforgettable time at the SF Masonic Auditorium! The venue is visually stunning—modern, clean, and intimate without feeling cramped. On a brighter note, I was relieved to see the elevator was accessible and actually functional—big win for anyone with mobility needs or carrying gear.

Unfortunately, my girlfriend had recently broken up with me and taken 17 of our small dogs. The singular 18th dog that she let me keep, unfortunately the runt of the litter missing both eyes, but having three extra ears, recently decided that it was fed up with me as well and walked itself to the vet to be put down without telling me.

As you can imagine, when I went to the Alameda Cineplex to see Sheep Detectives, I was very hopeful that it would be a light-hearted movie to raise my spirits, even though I was devastated to be going alone. Unfortunately, when I got to the box office, they looked me dead in the eye, assessed my face very visibly, scanning top to bottom, and told me that I was apparently visibly too soft to handle the intense subject matter of the movie Sheep Detectives. After some light verbal abuse from all six employees and the manager commenting on my soft eyes and weak spirit that apparently manifested itself through my posture, I conceded to watch The Backrooms instead for a lighter movie that they deemed I could handle.

However, around 30 minutes into The Backrooms, I decided that it was not my cup of tea. Not all was bad about The Back Rooms, but  it was too liminal, and the character The Onion had an incredibly grating voice. Despite me being a large fan of the character Gorp, his presence was simply not strong enough in the movie to override my hatred of The Onion, so I decided to leave the theater and try to theater-hop into Sheep Detectives.

When I came into Sheep Detectives, the sheep were all crowded around Hugh Jackman's character, kicking him and beating him in order to initiate him into their gang. I was immediately drawn into the story. The leading sheep, played by Danny DeVito, was by far my favorite character. His dark and demented backstory really resonated with me, and my recent experience losing my job and my girlfriend and 18 dogs. Unfortunately, 13 27ft tall security guards each accompanied one of my ex's dogs, trained now as, fear sniffing attack hounds, all rushed into the movie theater and airlifted me out of my seat, while the dogs clung on me with their massive genetically modified jaws. They attacked me for my movie hopping, beating me relentlessly and throwing me out onto the curb. I can't type due to my lack of fingers on my right hand and lack of a left arm, so i am writing this using my new nuro-link, which gives me debilitating migraines when every i do a think. I have also lost one eye and 1.83 ears. I am currently writing this from the hospital where they charge 2,000,000 per ibuprofen on top of my massive other medical debts and other credit card debts accrued by my sensory deprivation tank addiction.

Side note: the movie popcorn hit hard.
Three stars.

The Pulse of the Third Wave (Minus the Screens)
Visiting Four Barrel on Valencia remains a must for anyone who values technical precision in their cup. What sets this location apart is the deliberate atmosphere: keeping the space Wi-Fi-free and spinning vinyl completely shifts the energy. Instead of a silent sea of laptops, there is actual conversation against the backdrop of the massive Probat roaster operating in the back, immediately connecting you to the production craft.
Behind the bar, the execution is spot-on. The espresso is consistently dialed in with a clean, bright acidity, and the microfoam on milk drinks is velvety and poured at the exact temperature required to preserve its natural sweetness. If you opt for a single-origin pour-over, the cup clarity consistently does justice to the specific tasting notes of the lot.
Despite the heavy foot traffic, the line moves efficiently, and the staff manages the rush without losing their approachable edge. It’s a San Francisco staple that successfully keeps both its technical standards and its classic Mission neighborhood character intact.

The coffee is delicious, though definitely not cheap—a medium latte will set you back about $8. We all wish a good coffee still cost under $5, but that’s just the reality these days. Overall, the atmosphere is great, the prices are reasonable for the area, and it’s the kind of place you want to come back to. And, of course, the quality of the coffee makes the experience even better.

The Marina Green is one of the most beautiful waterfront parks in San Francisco. When I first moved here years ago, and was still running regularly, I used to run by or around it several times a week. For a while, a group of us even met there to play soccer. It’s one of those places that really grows on you over time. What many people don’t realize is that this area used to be marshland (once called North Beach) and was later filled with debris after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. It then became part of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, which helped mark the city’s recovery. The nearby Palace of Fine Arts is the only major structure from that exposition still standing today.

A friend once pointed out that the area even served as an airfield in the 1920s, which is hard to imagine when you see it now. Today, it’s a wide, flat, open grassy space that’s perfect for all kinds of outdoor activities. On any nice day, you’ll see people jogging, walking their dogs, flying kites, or just relaxing with a picnic while taking in incredible views of the Golden Gate Bridge and Alcatraz Island.

In recent years, weekend food trucks and coffee vendors have become regulars, which is a nice bonus if you want a quick bite or caffeine fix. There’s also a marina right there, so it’s a great spot if you’re into sailing or just enjoy being near the water. Overall, it’s a simple park, but the combination of history, open space, and unbeatable views makes it one of the city’s best places to spend time outdoors.

A good place to come and relax on a sunny day and we’d recommend the having lunch option here!

What really sets Emporium apart is its sheer scale—multiple levels, a mezzanine, and plenty of room to move without feeling cramped, even on busy nights. Classic arcade games, pinball machines, billiards, and interactive digital games create constant movement and energy throughout the space. The lighting design is immersive, with purples, blues, and pinks reflecting off graffiti-style murals and architectural curves. Staff members are efficient and friendly, keeping lines moving despite the crowd. It’s a social space where strangers bond over games, pool matches, and shared nostalgia. top_reviews.content:
CuriOdyssey is one of the Bay Area’s best family-friendly destinations and such a perfect blend of science, nature, and hands-on learning. We had an amazing experience from start to finish. The entire space is thoughtfully designed to keep kids engaged while also making it enjoyable for adults.

What really makes this place special is the combination of interactive science exhibits and the rescued native wildlife exhibits. The hands-on activities were incredibly engaging and encouraged curiosity, problem-solving, and exploration. The exhibits are well-maintained, creative, and educational without ever feeling overwhelming.

The animal exhibits were limited. Seeing the owl and other rescued animals up close was fascinating, and it was clear how much care goes into their rehabilitation and education programs. It’s wonderful knowing that the experience is not only entertaining but also supports wildlife conservation and teaches kids about local ecosystems.

The outdoor areas are beautiful, spacious, and perfect for kids to explore. The setting inside Coyote Point adds to the experience, with plenty of fresh air and scenic surroundings. Staff members were friendly, knowledgeable, and clearly passionate about what they do, which made the visit even better.

This is an ideal outing for families looking for something both fun and meaningful. It strikes the perfect balance between play and learning, and it’s the kind of place that leaves kids excited, curious, and asking questions long after the visit. Recommended for anyone with young children in the Bay Area.

I visited Cinemark Century Hayward for the first time, and overall, it was a pleasant experience. I went to watch Dhundhar and had a smooth experience from the start. I had already booked my ticket online, so there was no hassle upon arrival. On a positive note, the restrooms were clean, which I appreciated.

top_reviews.content: I've run through this area nearly every day for the past decade.   It's amazing how many things have changed and how much has stayed the same.  Great animal watching, plant watching, and people watching year round, and at every hour.

I found the scenery beautiful, and saw some good birds while I was there, and some water birds. It was a pleasant experience.

With as populated as the Bay Area is, it can be more challenging than some might think to get a taste of nature without leaving the city. This takes me the Emeryville/Berkeley area where I had the opportunity in visiting "McLaughlin Eastshore State Park". There is no actual street address here but it is where University Ave. & W. Frontage Rd. meet. It is also about 1/2 mile from I-80 so it is quite easy to get to when traveling my car.

I had come here during the evening of Saturday 6/23/2022 at around 7:45pm. The weather was a comfortable 64°F while being crystal clear with no clouds in sight as well as no Bay Area fog for that matter. What makes this state park convenient is that they offer a sizable parking lot (which is free of charge) as well as several trash bins and a few porta potties within a mere 50 yards from the bay water and trails.

The hours of operation are from 5am to 10pm seven days a week. Since this is a protected open space preserve area, the park actually extends 8.5 miles along the East Bay shoreline from the Bay Bridge to Richmond, This includes tidelands along the waterfronts of Oakland, Emeryville, Berkeley, Albany, and Richmond. Since I-80 is a very heavily traveled highway, you can witness joggers, cyclists, and walkers exercising from a distance if you look close enough.

Since I arrive right before dusk to check out the sunset, I luckily parked a stones throw from the water, rocks, and sandy beach area. Since this area stretches a very long distance, it never seems super crowded as opposed to a way more densely popular park or bike trail. And if you arrive during the time I did, you can witness some of the most awesome sunsets in all of the Bay Area.

With the good things about this park, you also need to consider the not-so good things as well. On any given day, you will spot quite a few homeless people (in tents, sitting in cars, and even just sleeping on the streets). It is the grim reality of many that hit hard times. But for the most part, many people here are courteous and keep to themselves. I felt safe during my visit and was able to soak in some of that fresh bay air while enjoying a perfect sunset. With that said and done, I am going to give "McLaughlin Eastshore State Park" an above average four-star rating.

top_reviews.content: Strolled into bakery in the early afternoon, and was happy to find so many breads and rolls still available.  Tried the corn and cherry scone, and I adored it.  The scone was hearty, and the texture with the added corn meal made the mildly sweet cherries even better.  The volume of it was also formidable, so I loved it even more.  The whole wheat savory scone was cheesy and had the same rich, hearty texture of the sweet scone, and the flavors were balanced well with the onions and herbs.  Delicious in every bite.  The corn muffin had corn niblets scattered throughout, and it was delicious, but it was not that different from a basic store-bought corn muffin mix to my palate.  The Zampano was a lovely hybrid of hints of spice, buttery goodness, and chewy bread, so good warmed up with your beverage of choosing.  The staff member at the register was incredibly kind, and he helped me get through my purchase without any hangups.  I loved the overall laidback vibe of the store as well as how easy it is to grab what you’re after and get to the register.  Very bohemian and welcoming.  I will stop in for so many other breads that I want to sample.

Wanted to audit Arizmendi Bakery on Lakeshore Avenue as part of my ongoing evaluation of local Bay Area food spots and artisan bakeries. Instead of ordering online, I opted to place my order directly at the counter to experience their morning foot traffic flow.

The location itself is highly accessible, sitting just a short distance from I-580, and I found that paid street parking was easily available right along the commercial strip.

This is the first bakery I’ve audited where you select and bag your own fresh pastries and baked goods before paying at the register. The self-service procedure can get a bit hectic during busy morning hours and commuter rushes. I found myself moving out of the way a few times so more seasoned patrons could grab their items quickly. Since no tongs are provided—only small paper squares—I had to handle everything carefully to avoid damaging the delicate pastries. Personally, I would prefer tongs here; with the current setup, it is incredibly easy for someone's hand or arm to accidentally brush up against neighboring pastries while making a selection, especially if they aren't gripping the paper properly or if the paper doesn't slip easily as they reach into the display case.

They offer a few different sizes of bakery bags to choose from. After selecting my four morning items, I headed toward the exit to get in the checkout line. The register line moves extremely fast, and my wait was only about a minute. You are expected to remember exactly what you selected so you can dictate your menu items to the cashier. I struggled a bit remembering the specific names, but with a quick glance into the pastry bags, the clerk was able to ring them up efficiently. The vibrant neighborhood space is a high-volume hub filled with locals making quick stops for hot coffee, espresso, and morning treats.

As for the actual food quality, the sourdough cheese roll was just okay. It was a bit dry, and my partner and I both didn't care for the cheese flavor—definitely nothing spectacular for a spot known for sourdough crust. The plain butter croissant was a major disappointment; based on its appearance, it was the least appealing looking of all the ones I've tried so far on my bakery tour. It completely lacked any crispness or shattering effect and was the softest croissant I have encountered yet. It simply isn't something I can recommend to pastry lovers. While the inside aeration and crumb structure look nice, there were literally no crispy parts on the entire exterior, and there are far superior options for authentic French croissants in the Bay Area food scene.

On the sweeter side, the berry hand pie was nice, delivering a good, sweet fruit flavor and solid crust geometry. The fruit pastry (Tuesday's Diamond Danish special) was also pretty good, offering decent crispy layers all around, though it still wasn't quite crisp enough for my personal liking.

Ultimately, Arizmendi Bakery is a perfectly fine neighborhood staple for a quick morning pickup or a local coffee run if no other specialized bakery options are available, but certain technical elements fall short of elite baking standards.

While the pizza tastes great, I feel like they don’t have enough day-to-day variety. I’ve had various of their pastries, and sometimes find them a bit dense, or they don’t feel fresh when I bite into them. However, the pastries taste great from their danishes to chocolate coconut scones (although I found the scone to have too much chocolate for my liking, but that’s just my preference). Tables inside and outside don’t seem to be cleaned very often throughout the day as every time I’ve sat at a table there are crumbs.

Arizmendi gets a lot of hype but if we’re being honest this place is a treasure that I wish was commonplace.

The pastries alone are delicious, especially the sourdough cinnamon swirls. The cookies are above average. In fact so far I haven’t been disappointed by anything and I have eaten at most bakeries in the bay.

Their pizza is inexpensive and makes for a great lunch. I don’t mind they only have one flavor a day, it keeps me out of my rut. I usually get a slice and a small soup, which is also du jour. Their soups are all vegetarian, the same as everything else so they’re not as flavorful as I’d like but they’re satisfying and where else can you get a well rounded lunch for just over $10 anymore?

Bonus points for being a worker collective. You can taste the love

They call it pie but it is more of an empanada. It was delicious. The staff where wonderful too. Informing me on which days they make the pies. Glad this place is on my route

Stepping into Caffe Trieste feels like stepping back in time. We first went to the bar for drinks, and afterward we went to the register to purchase karaoke time. The employee assisting us, a man wearing glasses and a face mask, informed us that we could no longer purchase karaoke because the registers had already been closed. He explained that they stop taking karaoke purchases at 12:30 AM. What was frustrating was that the business advertises its hours as “7 PM – Close,” with closing time being 2 AM, yet there is no notice online or posted anywhere stating that karaoke purchases stop much earlier. When we asked where this policy was listed, the employee admitted it was not posted on the website. Naturally, this was confusing and disappointing, especially for paying customers who came specifically for karaoke. Unfortunately, the interaction itself was also unpleasant. The employee came across as dismissive and blunt rather than understanding or helpful. top_reviews.content:
I went on a Thursday night and there weren't too many people. Plenty of seating. Obviously a reservation is required for the main bar area but walk-ins are allowed in the library. You can make a reservation here on Google and receive your passcode by email. Upon entering get your ID ready and when the door opens give your entry code and last name.

I ordered the Pinkerton and Kate Warne. The Pinkerton was like an Old Fashioned and the Kate Warne was like a Negroni. Both drinks were phenomenal from the bartender that night named Danny. He was friendly to me and is a very skilled bartender. It was my first time visiting Bourbon & Branch but won't be my last. I recommend if you're looking for a lowkey Speakeasy with great drinks.

Sometimes all it takes is opening one unexpected door... only to discover another waiting behind it.
We stopped into Rickhouse after the World Cup simply looking for a great cocktail and some advice about another bar we hoped to visit that evening. The bartender pointed us toward three guys who had just walked in, and after chatting with them for a bit, one of them offered to see if he could add a little surprise to our reservation.
That surprise turned into one of our favorite memories from San Francisco.
Later that night, we arrived at Bourbon & Branch and were escorted into Wilson & Wilson Private Detective Agency—the hidden speakeasy inside the speakeasy. We were treated to an incredible experience, a surprise tour, and when we asked for the check, the bartender smiled and told us our drinks were on the house. That's when we learned the person we'd been talking to at Rickhouse earlier that day was actually one of the owners.
Rickhouse was already fantastic on its own. The cocktails were exceptional (we're still trying to recreate them at home), the bartenders were welcoming, and the atmosphere was exactly what we love. But it's the kindness and genuine hospitality that made this experience unforgettable.
We'll never forget the afternoon that one conversation at Rickhouse led us through a series of unexpected doors—and into one of our favorite travel memories.

My husband and I have been coming here since we were dating and it is always the most perfect way to the end the night. Service is always fantastic. They have an extensive drink menu, and the staff know it well, offer recommendations and guide you through it. The cocktails are excellent, with classics on the menu, as well as very unique combinations. You can tell there is quite a bit of craftsmanship in each drink. The cocktails are also priced well.

If you're looking for a fun, immersive experience that transports you straight back to the 1920s Prohibition era, this speakeasy-style bar is a must-visit. From the moment you arrive, it feels like you are stepping into a secret world. There's no sign - just a mysterious door and a doorbell. Ring it, give the password, and you're in.

Reservations are required, and the exclusivity adds to the charm. Once inside, you're seated at a cozy table and handed an impressively large cocktail and spirits menu. My friend and I went on a Saturday night around 9:30pm and were surprised by how relaxed and uncrowded it was.

The seasonal drink menu is incredibly creative, ad the staff were fantastic - patient, knowledgeable, and happy to walk us through the options. The service was top-notch, and the ambiance was spot-on for the era. Dim lighting, vintage decor, and a vibe that makes you want to stay awhile.

I tried a few cocktails, but the standout for me was the Heavy Artillery - bold, balanced, and unforgettable. There are a few house rules that help preserve the experience: 1. Be discreet with cell phone usage 2. No flash photography and 3. Remain seated and enjoy the era.

Overall, we had a fantastic time and would absolutely go back. It's not just a bar - it's an experience!

A huge shoutout to Leah for taking the time to learn what we liked and guiding us to the perfect cocktails for each of us. Also- thanks to the amazing bartender, who absolutely nailed every drink: They were some of the best cocktails we’ve had! The service and drinks were exceptional. We couldn’t recommend this speakeasy more!

top_reviews.content:
Whether you’re visiting California for the first time or you’re a local, don’t go anywhere else—Boudin Bakery Café is the place to be! The clam chowder in the sourdough bread bowl is amazing, the coffee is excellent, and the Dubai Chocolate Croissant is an absolute must-try.

Despite being in a busy tourist area, the service is fast (about 15–20 minutes), with plenty of indoor and outdoor seating and a family-friendly atmosphere.

A special shoutout to Douglas, the best manager! He’s always walking the floor, welcoming guests, and making sure everyone has a great experience. His leadership and friendly staff make every visit memorable.

Highly recommend

I'm a huge fan of Boudin Sourdough. Whenever I visit San Francisco's Pier 39, this is always one of my must-stop places.
Their freshly baked cookies are delicious, but my absolute favorite is the Clam Chowder served in a sourdough bread bowl. The chowder is hot, creamy and so flavorful and the sourdough bread is amazing. The bread bowl is large enough to share, making it perfect for two people.
This place is usually very busy, especially on weekends. We visited on a weekend too, but went close to closing time, so there was almost no line. They have plenty of indoor seating with lots of space, making it a cozy spot to enjoy a warm meal while escaping the chilly weather at the pier.
If you're visiting Pier 39, I highly recommend stopping here for a bread bowl, you won't regret it!

If you’re visiting Fisherman’s Wharf, Boudin is one of those classic San Francisco stops that’s worth experiencing at least once. The sourdough has been part of the city’s history for generations, and watching fresh loaves being prepared while enjoying lunch adds to the experience.

We grabbed a classic clam chowder served in the famous sourdough bread bowl along with a French Dip sandwich. The chowder was rich and comforting, but the fresh sourdough is really the star. The crust has that signature chew while the inside stays soft enough to soak up every bite of soup.

One surprise was the upstairs Bistro Boudin. It offers a full bar with local beer, wine, and cocktails, making it a relaxing place to escape the crowds after walking the Wharf. It’s easy to miss if you don’t know it’s there.

Even if you’re not stopping for a full meal, it’s worth walking through to watch the bakery, browse the fresh bread, and soak in a piece of San Francisco history. Expect crowds around lunchtime, but service moved efficiently and the food came out quickly.

Recommended: Clam Chowder in the Sourdough Bread Bowl, French Dip, and a local draft beer if you’re taking a break from exploring the waterfront.

Perfect spot to rest after watching the sea lions at Pier 39! Even on a weekday, it was super packed, but we managed to get a seat quickly by sharing a table—plus, the sofas are incredibly comfy. Honestly, the clam chowder had a bit too strong of a fishy/briny taste for me. However, dipping the sourdough bread into the hot soup was still comforting and nice. Great location and vibe, just be ready for the crowds!

This place has a rich history dating all the way back to the 1800s. Their sourdough is absolute top-tier! The clam chowder and sandwiches were also amazingly delicious. If you’re in San Francisco, this is a total must-visit.
