If you're in Oakland or the San Francisco area, you absolutely must visit this incredible gem! The experience is genuinely authentic and refreshingly unfiltered. Jill, the host, has transformed the lower level of her home into a museum that pays homage to the Black Panther movement, allowing visitors to explore its history and the various programs created to uplift communities.

She has preserved original newspapers from the Black Panther era, creating a rich educational atmosphere. Jill is friendly, knowledgeable, and deeply passionate about sharing the positive impact of the Black Panthers on both local and global communities.

I discovered this treasure by chance, not realizing that it was her home upstairs and a museum downstairs, so I recommend scheduling an appointment to ensure you receive a proper tour. It’s conveniently located just 2 blocks away from the Black Panthers' national 4th headquarters and 1 block away a statue of Huey P. Newton, along with numerous murals outside of Jill’s home and throughout the area.

I'm so glad I had the opportunity to visit. I encourage everyone to experience this museum and consider donating to support Jill’s efforts in continuing to educate others about this significant movement. It's truly a must-see!

Coming here with my educator union after visiting Black Joy Parade. The Women Black Panther Museum was very empowering to visit.

We got a stellar tour the owner Jill whom bought it in 2000. She informed us that she had it to empower her self and the community of shining the light on Black Women that shine their light in their communities and are role models.

This is her way of resistance and made it with the context to ensure everyone in the neighborhood is acknowledged by saying hi to them. This was very uplifting as no one is erased.

I really appreciated the tour and was surprised to see the Turkeys 🦃 roaming freely! And a walk away is the Huey Statue.

Thanks for having us Jill!

We had an amazing experience visiting the Osher Rainforest at the California Academy of Sciences.

It was very enjoyable walking through the rainforest exhibit and seeing all the different plants and animals. One of the highlights was the water area at the bottom with fish, which added a lot to the experience.

There were also many butterflies throughout the exhibit, which made it feel very immersive.

The walkway was clean and well maintained during our visit.

Overall, it was a beautiful and memorable exhibit to explore.

The Osher Rainforest is one of the biggest highlights of the California Academy of Sciences. It’s mainly known for its free flying butterflies, but you will also find macaws, fish, spiders, and other creatures in this rainforest’s ecosystem. Stepping into this exhibit will truly make you feel like you’ve transported yourself to the rainforest, with its tall trees and hot, humid climate. They’ve really decorated this place well.  There are lots of picturesque spots, and on the top floor, you can even watch butterflies going through their beginning stages. The butterflies that flutter about come so close, that it feels as if they might land on you- which actually happened to one of my family members once. It’s pretty magical. 5/5.

As soon as you walk inside the recreated rainforest, you will be hit by the difference in humidity and temperature. The recreated rainforest is so beautiful and astonishing.

There are so many free living butterflies 🦋 and spiders 🕷️ roaming around in the area. In the middle of the hall, there is a small lake where tourists can see big fishes, a glimpse of the aquarium underground.

As you walk along the railing, you will see different species of insects and reptiles up to level 3. The exit is located on level 3, where the elevator will take you down to the aquarium underground to exit the rainforest. Make sure there is no butterflies or anything else attached to you before leaving.

The Rainforest Dome is the busiest spot of the building. There’s always a long line, but once you join, it goes by very quickly. Inside, the ambient air is warm and humid. Lots of butterflies fly inside this ecosystem. At the end of the tour you find yourself looking at a mirror, making sure no butterflies attach to your clothing. A fun experience.

So many things to see and different topics to learn about! Feel like the regular ticket price of $45ish is a lil pricey but once you're in you understand why. If you're a tourist the CityPass C3 bundle is a really good deal.

Well, what can I say about this place?
Number one, it was free.
Number two, the staff were very kind and friendly.
Number three, wonderful historical exhibits.
Number four, the Happy Birthday Oscar exhibit was quite moving and a wonderful tribute to a man who did not deserve to die at the hands of the police.
Overall, I enjoyed the experience at this museum. I look forward to possible expansion and can’t wait to come back in the future.

The Black Panther Party Museum, Oakland

As someone who went to Merritt College, I had learned about the history of the Black Panther Party from there. Merritt College has many photos and historical documents there that I wanted to learn more about it.

The Black Panther Party was founded in 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale. They met at Merritt College in Oakland. The movement started out small in Oakland’s Black communities, starting with feeding young children to opening up clinics for people of all ages.

Huey also went to China and met with many politicians and famous people there, the black and yellow community united together and not a lot of history mentions that.

This museum is located in Downtown Oakland, it is pretty small and has another room dedicated to Oscar Grant as well. The museum is free but accepts donations. The staffs were friendly and greets you when you walk in.

Would go again if I’m in the area.

The Oakland Museum has a small area about the Black Panther party as well, but it’s paid admission.

I visited the Black Panther Museum in Oakland today and left with a much deeper understanding of this pivotal movement in American history. Located in the heart of the city where the Black Panthers were founded, the museum does an excellent job of presenting the Party’s full story, not just the imagery most people know, but their community programs, like a complimentary breakfast for children, health clinics, and education initiatives. The exhibits are thoughtfully curated, featuring original photographs, newspaper clippings, and personal artifacts that bring the 1960s and 70s to life. What struck me most was how the museum humanizes the Panthers’ members, showing them as organizers and activists working to address real problems in their communities: poverty, police brutality, and lack of access to basic services. The staff are knowledgeable and passionate, happy to answer questions and provide context. Whether you’re familiar with this history or just learning about it, the museum offers a valuable perspective on a movement that shaped Oakland and influenced social justice efforts nationwide. It’s a small space but packed with powerful stories that deserve to be told. Highly recommend for anyone interested in civil rights history or in better understanding Oakland’s legacy of activism.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
Such a great museum and piece of history. They are expanding the museum. Will definitely be back for to see that. If you are in town make sure to stop in

The Cube is such an exciting addition to SF's art scene! Opened October 25, 2024, this is the new home of the San Francisco Art Institute, relocated from their previous location to this stunning five-story modernist building at 345 Montgomery Street. The exhibition space has more than doubled from 11,000 to 26,000 square feet, and the transformation is incredible.

The building itself is a work of art - originally the flagship Bank of America branch from 1971, redesigned by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill with a dramatic five-story atrium featuring grand staircases and cantilevered walkways. Located right at the corner of California and Montgomery Streets in the heart of the Financial District, it's super accessible by public transit.

What I love most is that admission is completely free! They focus on experimental contemporary art exhibitions that rotate regularly, often addressing social and cultural issues. No permanent collection, which keeps things fresh and dynamic. They also offer free workshops on weekends which is a nice touch.

Open Wednesday-Sunday 11am-5pm, with extended Thursday hours until 7pm. I'd recommend visiting Thursday evenings when it's less crowded. Perfect to combine with other nearby art venues like SFMOMA for a full art day. This transformation of a vacant bank into vibrant cultural space really represents downtown SF's renaissance!

Super excited to visit this museum. We all came from different parts of the city using public transportation and it was super easy to get to. It blends in and easy to miss as it’s tucked in the corner at the bottom of the BofA building at the corner of Montgomery. The displays are on 2 floors. They have a makers section so great of you have budding little ones who want to create something. Best of all…it’s free!

I am so grateful we have places like ICA SF in San Francisco. Art is extremely important in today’s society, where technology is overpowering creativity and empathy and understanding is becoming increasingly rare. Art is a universal tool for learning; about other perspectives, about history, and just about humanity in general, which is why I’m so glad that ICA SF makes it free and accessible to all.

The building occupied by ICA SF is just as beautiful as the art held within it, which is fitting. It shares the block with another wonderful building, 555 California Street, and is attached to the concourse. All of the art on display when I visited was impressive and moved me in one way or another. I liked that the spaces around the pieces correlated with the art displayed, that’s something I don’t see a lot in other art museums. My favorite exhibit of the three I saw had to be the Midnight March exhibit. Mainly because the figures were cute, but also because it was based off of a Japanese folktale. As an Asian, it’s always inspiring to see art surrounding Asian experiences and history, and I think we need more of it. There was also an area near the back where visitors could make art, and I had a great time creating as well as seeing others’ creations. There were also areas to read books, and restrooms.

The only reason I give ICA SF 4 stars is because I think it could use more art! I know that free admission is already very generous, but there were empty spots here and there which I thought could totally use a display. I also think ICA SF could have more potential if the upper three floors were used, but I’m guessing there is some kind of barrier to that. Lastly, there are occasional clanking sounds coming through the walls of the building due to it being next to the underground parking garage, but that is a minor issue that can’t really be fixed.

Overall, I’m so happy I stumbled across this place. 4/5.

top_reviews.content: We had the barn burner and the avocado toast, along with a hot mocha and a hot chai latte. My husband asked for the biggest mocha they make, which is 12 oz for all hot beverages. The food was delicious. Our only issues were his bacon practically shattered and the crust on my toast was really hard. The music is very loud and they were playing preschool songs, but there was at least one baby present, so it was endearing.

Caffe Central is a local cafe with multiple locations throughout the San Francisco Bay Area. What sets them apart from other cafes is their dedication to fresh ingredients and locally roasted coffee beans. Although their beans are globally sourced, the business partners with a local Pacifica business (Soul Grind Coffee) to roast their coffee beans (we love local businesses supporting each other)!

This particular location is conveniently located near UCSF Mission Bay, UCSF Bayfront, and the Chase Center, which makes it a perfect spot to stop-by and great a bite to eat or a coffee to-go. I tragically forgot to bring my lunch to work one afternoon, but was fortunate to learn that Caffe Central was just a quick walk away from me. I placed an order for an acai smoothie and a turkey avocado BLT via DoorDash for pickup (to time it with my lunch break), and was notified when my order was ready to pick-up (right on time).

Upon reaching their storefront, I was pleasantly surprised with how spacious and airy it was inside. There was plenty of seating and the wide windows let plenty of sunlight in, making it a great spot to stop and enjoy a bite. Unfortunately, I couldn't enjoy my meal in-store as they were closing, so I went on the hunt for somewhere else to sit and enjoy my food (if I had the time I would have definitely enjoyed my food in-store).

Their turkey avocado BLT features smoked turkey, bacon, cheddar cheese, arugula and mayo-pesto all on an acme baguette (it comes with tomato too, but I took that out). The sandwich was perfect - exactly what you expect when ordering a sandwich like this. all the ingredients tasted fresh and delicious, especially when paired with the creamy mayo-pesto and the crunchy acme baguette. The acai smoothie was equally tasty, and the acai flavor wasn't overwhelmed by the other smoothie ingredients. I guess you can say I was almost glad to have forgotten my lunch at home on this day, since I was able to enjoy a delicious meal like this!

I'd definitely recommend checking out Caffe Central the next time you find yourself at/near any of their locations and craving a bite to eat or something to sip on.

NOT NICE GUYS!!!
We will not be returning, even though the atmosphere is nice and the staff seemed friendly.

The reason is simple: be very careful when paying your bill.

Our bar tab was $90, and we didn't realize until afterward that a 20% gratuity had already been added to the bill. Then, when paying, the receipt again asks you to leave a tip with checkboxes for 20%, 25%, or 30%. Since we didn't notice the automatic gratuity, we selected 25% (another 30 bucks), thinking we were leaving the usual tip.

In the end, we unknowingly paid 45% in tips.

The most frustrating part is that we're apparently not the first people this has happened to. We later found a review from last year describing the exact same experience. If multiple customers make the same mistake, the payment process is clearly misleading.

This feels deceptive and leaves a very bad impression. A restaurant or bar should make it obvious when gratuity has already been included, instead of prompting customers to tip again in a way that's easy to miss.

Great atmosphere, but because of this experience, we won't be coming back.

top_reviews.content: This is a one of a kind experience that one of our family members has been dreaming of visiting for years. I have never had the chance to see, smell, and appreciate such unique flavors and fragrances in my life. If someone is a perfume or fragrance enthusiast, this  is an amazing experience. There are incredible opportunities to take home some of the samples and mixtures as arranged by the staff and overseen by the proprietor, Mandy Aftel and her family. She made it a personal goal to greet and speak to each guest. Reservations are important and allow no less than an hour to 90 minutes for a visit. Worth it for the olfactory curious adventurers!

A must do for anyone interested in perfumery, especially naturals! Mandy Aftel + her family created this completely unique experience with decades of collecting information on herbs + scents.

Aftel Archive was amazing! Truly a personalized and intimate experience from beginning to end.. the owner, Mandy Aftel, was incredibly hospitable and educated us on the process and intracacies of perfume-making. Will definitely visit when in town again!

It's a museum on scents and perfumes. There is a small rare book collection on perfume recipes, perfume ingredients, scent smelling, etc.  Some books date back to 1820.  I found the books quite interesting - easy to read.  I never given a thought that there was a science in making perfumes and scents.

The museum is inside a cottage that looks like it was built in the mid 1900. It's small, cute with well thought out displays and simple to understand signage. The family owned staffed museum is friendly and informative.  Inside, you are required to wear a mask to smell perfume samples and a glove to touch artifacts, open drawers and books. Outside you get a paper sniffer to smell bottled perfumes and a black cloth to clean your nostrils from smells. Admission is $25 per person including smelling/touching packet.  You will receive a brief introduction and then you are free to guide yourself in the museum.  The museum is only open on Saturdays with reservations.

Mandy, the woman, who created this museum, authored several books on scents and perfumes.  She will sign your books upon request. My favorite display is the 19th century clove ship from Indonesia.  It's so intricate - something to appreciate for the person who built it.  Scents are natural essences of animals, flowers, fruits, trees and whatever.

The ones that didn't feel strange were Figure 2 right: Crab Remoulade and Figure 3 left: Gold Standard (decent).
For those who like sweet and savory combinations: Figure 2 left Brusco and Figure 5: Ham & Fig (I quite liked these).
For those who prefer savory (very American cold sandwich style): Figure 4: Muffuletta (I personally didn't like this one).
For those who like sweet and sour flavors: Figure 3 right: Tangerine & Burrata (I didn't dislike this one).
Overall, it's a good option when you want something simple and not too large in portion size, similar to Riceful – something I might want to go back to occasionally, but not something I need to eat every day.

Came to San Francisco looking for a solid early breakfast burrito and found ourselves wandering the Mission at 6:30am—only to realize most places don’t open until 8. Then we stumbled upon Cafe Gonzales… and wow, what a gem!

This spot is hands down one of the best burrito joints in SF. No exaggeration.

I ordered the B2 and it was next-level: three perfectly scrambled eggs, fresh spinach, melted cheese, creamy avocado, and hearty black beans, all wrapped in a warm, soft wheat tortilla that tasted homemade. What brought it all together? Their incredible salsa—bright, flavorful, and just the right amount of kick.

Everything was exceptionally fresh, the portion was generous, and the flavors were beautifully balanced. You leave feeling full, happy, and already planning your next visit.

If you’re in SF and need an early breakfast that hits all the right notes, Cafe Gonzales is your spot. Burrito lovers—don’t miss this place! 🌯

FM Smith Park — Oakland

This park is a hidden Oakland treasure!
It doesn't have the biggest or newest playground, but it has everything (but a bathroom) you'd want in a park!
With two play areas separated by a big grass field, sand, shade, basketball and a garden... Add this one to your list!

On the other side of the park is a smaller play area geared towards younger kids. It has steps, a slide, and a ladder. This play area is on sand and has many community donated toys to add to the park time fun.
The huge grassy area between is w great place to kick a ball, throw a frisbee, play fetch with your dog (signs say no dogs but they were there), or have a picnic below the redwoods or at one of the picnic tables with bbq.

top_reviews.content:
Hawk Hill according to SF Rec&Park website is “a magnificent remnant hilltop dune with ocean views of southwestern San Francisco. The shifting sand supports a wide variety of dune plants, including the locally rare California croton and the San Francisco wallflower.” However, the posted park hours and location is inaccurate and in fact is contradicted by the fact that there are no designated trails or known public access. 😳
I have “canvassed” the area surrounding the Hark Hill for weeks and the following are my two cents for alternative routes to discover the Hawk Hill:
Ⅰ. 14th Avenue Route:
⓵ Muni 48 or 66 stops at 14th Avenue and Rivera right in front of Herbert Hoover Middle School{“No Trespass” sign posted}
② Muni 6 stop at Quintara and 14th Avenue then climbing downhill⚠️very steep⚠️on 14th to reach Rivera.
③ Alternatively, you can climb up on Quintara Steps {about 7 floors} or Rivera Steps {not yet climbed} to connect 14th or 13th Ave (Funston) walking downhill to the Hawk Hill.

Ⅱ. 9th Avenue en route San Marcos:
On that day I was catching Muni Line 6 from Main Library got off at Pacheco the cut through Oriole Way {about 5 floors} to Cragmont [broken 11th Ave] then climbed on steep remnant 10th Ave {about 10/12 floors} to Mendosa, Mesa, Santa Rita to San Marcos. It’s such an amazingly seclusively tranquille neighborhood reminds of San Mateo Park. Miraculously, there is a public unnamed steps to reach Dorante to catch L on Taraval through Cortes. [I was wondering whether all these street names ended with S instead Z are Portuguese explorers like Aguello [de facto 1st Avenue] and Cabrillo. {Double L in Portuguese does not pronounce same in Spanish if you know what I mean.😉]
Enjoy exploring The City while hiking😄
PS Before West Side was developed winds deposited sand on Hawk Hill from surrounding dunes in Sunset. Now dunes are all gone except “Sunset Dune” 😂 leaving no source of sand to replenish Hawk Hill. Let’s keep away from the trail of Hawk Hill. 🙏

top_reviews.content: An incredible spot, really unique and different. Whether you're an aerial performer or an admirer of the performing arts, they cater to both performers and spectators with genuine warmth and inclusivity. A review of sorts, to whoever might be interested in performance, creativity or live theatre....

Anyone who has searched for a performance space in San Francisco will tell you that it is a monumental endeavor not be take on by the faint of heart!  Depending on your project, your artistic vision, your personal stamina and, not least, your budget, you will eventually come to the conclusion that, regardless of its reputation for open-mindedness and creativity, it is practically impossible to find a place in the windy city  that is truly workable.

I, though I am notably stubborn in certain regards, had, after searching for and visiting a multitude of possible locations for just about half a year, come to the conclusion that what I was looking for did not, in fact, exist.

I had just one more theatre to look at before completely giving up....Thank goodness I had not, because the minute I stepped into Little Boxes Theatre, I knew I had finally arrived at the place I was looking for!!!

There is an air about the place that is very hard to describe.  Located in a warehouse near 3rd St.,  there is no exterior indication that would lead you to believe how warm, welcoming and compelling the place will feel once you get inside. High ceilings, tiered comfortable seating, a large open performance area, one senses an artistic openness, spatial malleability and a naturally inclusive intelligence to the space the minute you walk in the door. The same characteristics with which I would describe the folks who are the heart and soul of this theater - Aaron and Christina!    Dancers, models, photographers, producers, entrepreneurs, set design/builders, directors, creative collaborators, Aaron and Kitty (Christina) can make almost anything happen in that space.

And we did!  Though an opera had never been produced at Little Boxes before our production, with the help of Aaron, Kitty and a host of others, we produced a chamber version of Verdi's Macbeth that was unlike any other!  Though there were challenges, of course, the theater proved to be an amazing place to bring that provocative musical story to life.

Little Boxes Theater is an extraordinary, completely unique place.  Anything you can imagine can be created there. As long as Aaron and Kitty are there, Teatro Mistral will be creating performances there too!

Vismaya Lhi - Artistic Director/Teatro Mistral
Teatro Mistral

top_reviews.content:
This was a fun find for my kids and I. Typically I steer away from claw machine games because let's face it, you lose more than you win. With the incentive of receiving 2 plushies with a minimum game purchase amount, it alleviated the anxiety of walking away with nothing to show for my kids. The space was well lit and clean. We were the only patrons during the last hour of day.

Heads up- once the claw retracts and moves back towards the prize drop zone, it shakes A LOT and we end up losing the plush animal any way. Occasionally we managed to get 2 or 3 wins. As I mentioned earlier, you're guaranteed two plushies when you purchase a minimum game card amount, so that made the losses more manageable.

Overall, it was a fun experience and I'd take my kiddos there again. The gentleman that helped us was friendly and reassured us about the two guaranteed plushies to put us at ease so we can try to enjoy our time.

All machines were almost empty. Card machines were not working so we can play for free then choose to keep or not what we got. After playing we realized each stuffed animal was $10, so we charged $20 for 2. I feel it’s too much. Though we can play unlimited, we didn’t feel to do so because of atmosphere. It was not fun.. and we do not come again.

For such a concept, it was weird location, a very affluential neighborhood so I'm not sure if the location will be popular with this crowd? They're very nice people and went out of their way to trade with my son what keychain he wanted. The machines are colorful and cool but at 20.00 I left with a one keychain :(

Went to the soft opening today of Starbunni with some family, and the vibes were so cute and fun and the plushies were so cute! Most arcades with claw machines have cheap looking stuffed animals and prizes but this one had a range of the cutest plushies and even Sanrio ones! I also found out the claw machines were all imported from Japan which is awesome!

They also have a great selection of blind boxes all Sanrio themed that are so addicting, and cute keychains for sale!

I can’t wait for the grand opening as I was told that their photobooth will be up and running! They also will soon open their customizable plushie station where you can customize your own plushies with different clothes and shoes on a huge tv screen! On top of that, they plan to eventually sell Pokémon cards, Sonny Angels, & Smiskis which is super exciting!

The pricing is also very affordable for the credits you receive to play the claw machines, and I love how they let you switch out your winnings to the plushies they have up front if you wish to do so! Definitely plan to come back again with more friends and family :)

I enjoyed learning more about the Alamo, Danville and San Ramon areas from the past. I was familiar with some history but this fills in many gaps, with its rich collection of research books you can read there.

top_reviews.content: What an interesting museum between Fishermans Wharf and Ghirardelli Square. So much information packed into the space. Some interactive exhibits too! Free admission with donation requested 🙏

Such great quality from a museum with completely free admission! The museum is rather small, encompassing a single floor with 2 or 3 subsections, but I managed to spend about 40 minutes in there. Eyes seem like a boring subject, but they make it interesting! Almost everything was interactive in some way and they have numerous artifacts on display, making it enjoyable and educational for both kids and adults. There was even an employee guiding a group of families when I visited.

The only downsides I can think of is the lack of bathrooms and one of the interactive buttons not functioning, but that is really nitpicky. You can find public bathrooms at Ghirardelli Square.

Overall, if you’re looking for something quick, new, and free to do in the area, stop by the Museum of the Eye. 4/5.

I passed by this museum many times and never went in until someone asked me to attend a docent tour of this museum.  I am glad I went.  it was a refresher of my high school/college physiology/anatomy classes.  It details in simple language for all ages to understand. The graphics and pictures help explain. Anyone interested in learning the history of eye care and how it functions/diseases/etc., this is the absolute place to visit.  Admission is free and staff are friendly, knowledgeable and eager to help.  Most artifacts are donated.  It's an interactive museum where you can explore.  Attached pictures are from the special exhibit they currently have - Asian - which is retiring at the end of this month.  The museum changes their "special exhibit" frequently.  I especially enjoy the timeline of written recorded ophthalmology.
Interesting museum and a hidden gem in SF. Lots of history of ophthalmology and some recent scientific advancements. Also, the admission is completely for free.

Nice small exhibit. Very friendly lady at the entrance. It is not worth a detour, but if you are curious and nearby, why not. The level of explanation is either too light or too heavy; the exhibit doesn’t feel very cohesive.

top_reviews.content:
My milkshake brings all the boys to the yard...
And honestly, yeah, I can see why from the start.
This place has a ton of variety to choose,
Different sizes, flavors, and full-on sugar moves.
Go for the large with the toppings stacked high,
That thing is big enough to split, no lie.
It’s less of a dessert and more of an event,
The kind you order once and then feel financially spent.
They’ve even got cookie dough scoops on the side,
For people who want to skip the shake ride.
Just straight-up dough in its own little section,
Which is either dangerous or a great invention.
The flavors rotate, so it stays pretty fresh,
Seasonal options slide in with the rest.
So even if you’ve gone once, there’s still a reason
To circle back around for the next weird season.
You can order at the screen if you want to move quick,
Or talk to someone up front and do the human pick.
Service was nice, which helps when the menu’s a beast,
Because narrowing it down is not exactly a peaceful feast.
Bathrooms are down a shared hallway away,
Not a huge deal, just useful to say.
And the mason jar mug is yours to keep,
Which somehow makes the sugar rush feel cheap.
So yes, the shakes are wild, over the top, and hard to ignore,
Basically dessert with a little bit more.
If you get the loaded large, bring backup to your yard,
Unless your dentist needs a new boat and you want to help him charge.

I ordered the pecan praline shake and it was thick enough where you will eventually need a spoon to finish.  The staff is friendly and helpful with selections and I can't wait to return.

The Yard
TLDR:
Overall: Fun, extremely sweet (although pricy) over-the-top milkshakes
My Order: Brookie Batter Specialty Milkshake
Price Breakdown: $23.90 (including tax, etc for a pricier one of the milkshake options)
Portions: Enough to share one milkshake between two people
Halal/Vegetarian Friendly: Not applicable, though dairy-wise there might be vegan options but I'm not 100% sure, do check on that!
Would get again: I am very tempted to try the strawberry cheesecake or the oreo one, but probably would get the bowl instead of the milkshake next time.

So this was one insane milkshake. After seeing pictures online of these over-the-top fantasy-esque milkshakes and realized there was a new location in Berkeley, I was very intrigued and finally made my way down. We got the specialty milkshake (mostly bc it comes with the souvenir glass that they let you clean and take home after) and I promise you this is enough for two people for sure. There were a lot of moving parts in our Brookie Batter Specialy Millshake, cookie dough icecream, a brownie, a cookie, lots of chocolate chips, a definitely very pretty dessert.

This was a very sweet dessert (almost needed to wash down with water at some point) and we were incredibly full by the end of it, even when we shared it. The flavors were very fun at first, but as we continued, it did get a bit overwhelming and the tastes merged together a bit. The milkshake part ended up being a bit more refreshing than the rest of it. And unfortunately but understandably the price is quite a bit steep for the milkshake, but this was a very complex treat with lots of different components that made it a bit more worth it. The staff was also lovely and helpful in getting utensils and choosing a milkshake.

Overall, definitely not trying to be a regular here (for the sake of my health 😅), but will be back to try the other flavors (in bowl form) at some point. I may add a star if the oreo one fulfills my heart's desires.

I ordered the Mint Madness Specialty Milkshake for $20, and I honestly don’t think it was worth it at all. The toppings were not nearly as generous as I expected: just whipped cream, one brownie piece, a scoop of cookie dough, one piece of Oreo, and some chocolate chips at the bottom of the shake. They didn’t even blend the chocolate chips into the milkshake — they just poured them straight in from the package, so they wouldn’t come up through the straw. You can also tell the ingredients are pretty average. The chocolate lacked that rich cocoa-butter aroma, and the whipped cream wasn’t good either.

I also ordered the Triple Chocolate milkshake, which was $10. The chocolate flavor was not rich at all, and it didn’t even have a nice milky taste. Compared with Shake Shack, it’s nowhere close. On top of that, the prices are really expensive. Other than looking good visually, it has no real strengths. I wouldn’t recommend it, and I definitely won’t be coming back.

We ordered a drink at last call and around 10 minutes later we were informed we had to leave. The security guy said he’d check with the bartender. They agreed to let us stay to finish our drink. As we left at 1 they closed the door lights came on and at least 6 people were sitting at the bar having drinks. It appeared the staff just wanted to get done and have drinks with their friends. It’s a bad look when paying customers are asked to leave and friends stay. Each round for our group was around $40. We would have had at least two more. How many others would have had another round too. Joe kick money do they lose weekly doing this. Plus now that we know you can’t count on the hours we may choose to go to other spots we know stay true to their listed hours. Again if they had closed and were cleaning and no one was there I’d probably be more understanding but to usher everyone out and have 5 or 6 people who i did not see working that night (maybe they are staff and had the night off) sitting at the bar after we were told they were closed was a bad look. Considering i bought round 1 and it was $42 before tip and we had at least 4 more rounds after that one. We spent over 200 on the night. I wouldn’t want to run customers like that off.

The service was phenomenal, created and led by a kind and gentle mastermind. The food and pastries were SO delicious.

Don’t even get me started on the coffee. The coconut cappuccino and the Kopi avocado have a grip on me. So yummy I had to get some to go and share with family.

I move out of Berkeley this week and I now look forward to returning and indulging in the exceptional flavors of everything and the colorful space. Wouldn’t be surprised to come back to finding a line down the block to try it.

I scheduled a blow out for the morning of my birthday and wrote that as a note in the comments. I was greeted brusquely by Janee with “are you Alexandra?” No “have you been here before? Would you like something to drink? Do you need to go to the bathroom? Happy birthday!”  Etc… I had booked an extra 10 minute scalp massage so when I glanced at my watch as I sat in the shampoo bowl I noticed it was 10:03. She shampooed my hair and then lightly layed her index fingers over my forehead (?) then conditioned my hair, rinsed and wrapped a towel around my hair and when I sat up my watch said 10:09 so I figured she had forgot about the massage.

We discussed that I wanted big bouncy blow out waves but I stated my hair didn’t hold a curl well so it was ok if the curls were a little tighter. She then turned me away from the mirror for about 25 minutes and when she turned me around I had tight Shirley temple-esque curls. I instinctively reached up to touch them and she said offered half heartedly to “run her fingers through my curls” which I stated I could do on my own.

When I went to check out, I clarified the extra charge for the scalp massage since it had been so brief and she was clearly irritated, but the other staff person said the charge could be taken off. The sign by the register suggested $12 as a tip if you “liked it “ seeing as I DISLIKED it, I added a $10 tip to which she rolled her eyes at me and still included the charge for the “massage” which I awkwardly had to correct a second time. By the time I finally paid I was shaking- I felt so uncomfortable, frustrated and irritated and sad that my birthday was starting out on such a bad note. Needless to say, I won’t be back.

Review for Scarlett Lounge (Last Night’s Experience)

I don’t usually write reviews, but after what happened last night, I feel like I have to speak up. I went into Scarlett Lounge hoping for a good time, maybe a drink or two, and instead I walked out feeling completely dismissed and honestly a little embarrassed.

The bartender Joanne was the main reason the night went downhill. From the moment I sat at the bar, she made it painfully obvious that serving me was not a priority at all. I tried to be patient — I understand bars get busy — but this wasn’t a busy situation. This felt personal, like I was invisible.

Joanne spent most of her time chit-chatting with a group of customers, laughing and leaning over the bar, fully engaged with them while I sat there waiting. I tried to make eye contact. I even raised my hand politely at one point. She looked directly at me… and then just turned back to her conversation as if I wasn’t even there. It felt disrespectful, like my presence didn’t matter.

When she finally decided to come over, there was zero effort to be accommodating. No smile. No “sorry for the wait.” Not even basic courtesy. Just a cold, quick, “What do you want?” like I was bothering her by trying to order a drink. Her energy was so dismissive that it instantly killed the whole vibe of the night for me.

I’ve been to all kinds of bars — upscale spots, dives, lounges — and I’ve never felt so brushed off by a bartender. It wasn’t the crowd or the atmosphere. It was the lack of customer care from Joanne that ruined everything. Maybe she treats regulars well, but if you’re a new face, don’t expect much.

Last night was supposed to be fun. Instead, I left annoyed, disappointed, and honestly questioning why I even gave this place a chance. I definitely won’t be coming back anytime soon.

This park is new. It officially opened on March 2, 2018. It has turned an awkwardly shaped and sloped piece of land into a nice neighborhood amenity.

At the time I write this review (March 3, 2018), a fair amount of the park is still fenced off to allow the initial groundcover to take hold.

The biggest attraction will, I think, be the playground structures. There are two sets, 1 fenced and designed for kids under 5, the other unfenced and designed for ages 5-12 (per the signs posted).

I doubt Peggy Thompson Pierce Street Park will become a significant destination for people who don't live within walking distance for the following reasons:
1) It's just too close to the freeway. The freeway dominates all views and contributes significant noise. There is no way that anyone might call this park "peaceful" unless a major accident has stopped all freeway traffic!
2) Unless you have a handicapped placard, parking is on-street in an area that had nearly full on-street parking before the park was built. In other words, I don't recommend driving here!

With that said, I think there are three groups of people who will see this park as a great addition:
1) Families with young kids who live within walking distance
2) Bicyclists using Pierce Street (for whatever reason) as it provides a place to stop and rest a bit
3) Anyone who is nearby and needs to find a public restroom!

google.description: Built in 1869, this Italianate mansion houses a museum with period furnishings & decor.

top_reviews.content:
The Pardee Home Museum (Italianate architecture) was built by the Pardee family.  Three generations lived lived there from 1868 to 1981.  The last survivor put the home in a trust that is run by a Board of Trustees.  It's self-supporting and run by volunteers.  The father (made money in the mines, was an eye doctor and a California State Senator) and his son was Governor of California who made the poppy flower CA's state flower; reformed prisons;  and established the EBMUD.  All furnishings and collections are original and left intact.  The tour is about 1.5 hours. Tour was educational and interesting - it covers the entire residence of 3 floors.  The tour guide was nice and knowledgeable.  She kept the tour intense so you wanted to know more.  She gave insights and tibits of the family.  All questions were answered.

The afternoon tea is delightful.  The food is prepared from scratch with lots of love from the volunteers.  They were friendly, personable and thoughtful.  Since it was the day before Easter, they put some Easter bunny theme to the tea.  Just lovely people who made a delcious three course of food assortment.

I definitely recommend the tour to learn about Oakland history and to visit one of the last standing historical mansions.  Tea was authentic - no crust on the bread :)

Parse Family Museum was like a time capsule with incredible detailing and collections inside. Our work group was able to secure a private garden afternoon tea with 3 courses of goodies and all the english breakfast tea you could ask for. The women there were lovely and patient with us and even gave us each a thank you gift to take home. Following the tea and treats we took the tour which lasted a little over an hour sharing the homes history across 3 floors of unique treasures and facts. There is plenty parking both free and paid on both ends of the street just not directly out front. The ease of access as you come across the overpass made it all the better to get too! Definitely a place I will return to with family.

TL; DR: Great place to experience a tea party (by group reservation only). Interesting Victorian home museum in which to learn about local history, including that it was home to the first fulltime CA governor. House is chilly in cold months so wear layers, but the dinning room has a space heater during tea. Don't forget to bring cash for the donation box, it'd be appreciated :)
---
I visited here with a group for tea service. The entire thing from the set up, baking, and serving was beautifully orchestrated by friendly museum volunteers who delighted us with a lovely spread of tasty tea and baked goods in the historic home's dinning room.

Tea parties are the home museum's main source of income and a great place to celebrate special occasions or just have an outing with a group of friends. The service is hosted by reservation for groups only. There's a minimum number of attendees required. In the winter the max number of tea guests per party is limited to 12 (the size of the dinning room table). In warm weather, the max is closer to 40 people and its hosted in the patio. Check their website for info.

Our visit was concluded with a docent led tour of the house covering the story of the 3 generations of Pardees who lived there. The family was influential in politics, and was also active in medicine. The house is filled with thousands of family artifacts and collections, including some artwork by the talented Mrs. Pardee. There's definitely plenty to see and learn here.

For the sake of time, our tour didn't include a view of the room with old toys and human specimens (remember that least one Pardee was a physician). If you're curious, you could request a view from the docent. I actually was not aware of this room at all until a fellow tour goer asked about it.
Great home museum but the true highlight was the afternoon tea and the lovely ladies who served us and gave us the right amount of sass!

top_reviews.content:
Came in on the Fourth of July while I was in town visiting family and friends. We make it a point to stop here every year, and the plan was to meet everyone at the Benton a little later. I was out for a walk, so I stopped in about an hour early.

Since I knew I'd be having drinks once the rest of my group arrived, I decided to hold off on ordering one right away and instead paid for a game of pool to kill some time.

A few minutes into my game, the bartender came over and asked what I'd like to drink. I explained that I was waiting for the rest of my group and was planning to order later. She barked at me with Berkley lady energy that the pool table was for paying customers only and that I'd have to leave. I was surprised, since I had literally just paid to use the table. I said, "No problem, I'll finish my game," and left without making an issue of it.

I ended up messaging everyone in our group to meet somewhere else instead. In more than 20 years of working at bars, drinking at bars, and playing pool at bars, I've never heard of a paid table being for customers only.

Thankfully, the rest of the night was great. We ended up at Wally's, where the Diamond pool table is in much better shape and of much higher quality play. Then,  finished the evening at Lucky 13, which had an awesome atmosphere, great vibe, a great back patio, and friendly bartenders.

Until next year, Alameda. But, I think we can skip meeting in the middle here.

The bartender is very rude. They closed 15 minutes early without letting us finish our drinks or use the restroom.

top_reviews.content: First, many thanks to Jil who has created this amazing museum of Black Panther Party history. The mural on her house is stunning and powerful. Stepping inside you instantly learn about the legacy of community and public service that the Black Panther Party has done, from their free social programs to their liberation schools. I really enjoyed seeing the archives of Black Panther Party newspapers, including one that features a letter of solidarity from Japan, showing the global impact of the organization. If you’re ever in the area, visit and donate. If you can’t make it out but respect this effort, support with a donation. Support and protect this historical gem.

My partner and I were visiting San Francisco for a few days, and decided to make the trip over to Oakland to explore the history of the Black Panthers. It was absolutely worth it, and if you do the same, make sure you come here.

The museum is thoughtfully laid out, and is extremely thought-provoking. Importantly, it gives the women of the Black Panther Party the recognition they are due. A real highlight was the original copies of the newspaper ‘The Black Panther’ that we were able to look through. To read their own words and recordings of their own history provided incredible insight that is hard to find elsewhere. I found the tribute to Li’l Bobby, written by 18-year-old Belinda, especially moving.

We visited this mural and museum right after going to the other museum in town. This one was by far a better and more representative experience. It’s located in Jil’s home, and we were grateful to be hosted by her on short notice. After our visit, she also kindly pointed us in the direction of several significant sites in the neighbourhood.

I can’t thank Jil enough for taking the time to walk us through the exhibition. Thank you for opening your home to us and for this incredible museum in honor of the women of the Black Panther Party.
This history and space is so important to our history, thank you for sharing it.
A must visit when your in Oakland.

A true one of a kind gem, no visit to the Bay Area should be considered complete without a visit to the West Oakland Mural Project. It is a living historic space dedicated to social actions that originated in Oakland and changed the entire world. To be able to read history in the words of the people who made it, is something beyond an average museum experience. The interior is warm and filled with so much information, impeccably informative displays, reference materials, before we even get to the exterior where an incredibly moving and inspiring mural wraps around the building. Deeply inspired to share my experience, being from Oakland I have never been so moved by a historic space. Matching the beauty of the of the museum is its founder Jil, who generously greeted me, offered to answer any questions and at the end gave suggestions of other spaces to visit in Oakland. Off the record, I had already seen them and hers is by far the best.  She also suggested a walk which I took to see more murals in the neighborhood. If you are still reading this, stop and schedule a visit. It will change your life.

A friend visited this amazing museum while she was on a radical sabbatical and told me I absolutely had to go. Once I came to CA, it was the first place on my list and seeing the outside mural and the beautiful orange flowers growing in the entry way arch outside had me hooked. We met Ms Jil and put on our shoe covers and took a walk into and through a huge chapter of history that we had never heard. The Black Panthers were so much more than we know and we need to know. You have not visited San Francisco or Oakland if you miss the opportunity to visit this Women of The Black Panther Party Museum.

Kallista

top_reviews.content: One of the most peaceful hidden gems in Golden Gate Park! Three Gems is a stunning skyspace by James Turrell tucked into a grassy mound in the de Young's sculpture garden. You walk through a curved tunnel and enter this meditative circular chamber with an oculus opening to the sky. The way the natural light and subtle LED colors interact with the dome is mesmerizing — the sky's color shifts completely depending on the lighting. It's best at twilight when the LED colors cycle through pinks, purples, and blues, creating this magical experience. Completely free to visit and such a unique, contemplative space. Highly recommend visiting around sunset if you can catch the museum before closing

Cool spot to watch the light moves. It is located behind the museum, i entered through the cafe and then outside. Very cool installation and the acoustic there is amazing. Great spot to sit and listen to the world, watch the light moves and enjoy the structure.

The open space allowed me to fully immerse myself in Turrell's artwork and experience it in a way that I never have before.
The space creates a sense of calm and tranquility. It was almost meditative to spend time in there.
I highly recommend visiting a James Turrell open space  if you have the opportunity. It's a unique and free experience:)

This place hit something very personal for me — a childhood dream of an arcade where you don’t constantly pay per game. It’s a flat fee: you walk in and just play. No tokens, no timers, no pressure.

It works really well for adults and for kids. My wife and I had a lot of fun, and our kids were just as happy. There’s self-serve craft beer for the grown-ups, which somehow fits the arcade atmosphere perfectly.

The design is well done: neon signs, video displays, and a layout that feels intentional rather than chaotic. A few machines were broken, but there was still more than enough to play, and most of the games were in good condition.

The best part was how uncrowded it was. We had the place almost entirely to ourselves for nearly 2 hours as a family, which made the experience feel relaxed and special.

Overall, a great concept and a fun spot for a family outing where both parents and kids genuinely enjoy themselves. We’d happily come back.

I really like the Hot Wheels pinball machine that also vibrates. They have 4 TVs and 4 player consoles, got to play some Mario kart and some basketball. There’s some street parking and there are parking garages all around the area. You pay for a fee for an hour to play all of the machines but the pinball machines are $1 for each game.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

We recently hosted an 8th-grade graduation party at Pixels, and it could not have been more perfect. We had seven families and 53 guests, and the venue was ideal for a group of that size. Even with everyone there, the space never felt crowded, and the fun, energetic atmosphere made it the perfect place for our boys to celebrate this milestone together.

A huge part of our positive experience was working with Rob. From the very beginning, he was incredibly responsive, flexible, and easy to work with. Planning an event with multiple families can be complicated, but Rob made the entire process feel effortless. He accommodated special requests, communicated clearly, and genuinely wanted the event to be successful.

The food was great, the games kept everyone entertained, and everything ran smoothly from start to finish. The value was outstanding, especially considering we hosted such a large group.

Most importantly, the kids had an absolute blast. It was one of those rare events where both the kids and parents left happy.

Thank you, Rob and the Pixels team, for helping create such a memorable celebration. We would absolutely host another event here and highly recommend Pixels to anyone looking for a fun, stress-free party venue.

Prior to the development of the 'Claremont Court' subdivision, a spring at the top of the Garber St. hill flowed down and created a pond here.  It is said that in the summer, local farmers would bring their cattle to wallow in the cool waters.  The famed painter William Keith is said to have painted the pastoral scene.

With the initial mapping of the subdivision in 1906, a water company took over the spring, and a culvert was built, allowing the creation of the park.   It is reputed to be one of the first suburban residential subdivisions in the US.  The subdivision's development took place during the rapid transition from horses to automobiles.The subdivision initially featured a watering station for horses right in the middle of the gates on Claremont Blvd. The subdivision plan called for (coal) gas street lanterns,  but after the earthquake and fire in San Francisco the idea was discarded.  In some places, the abandoned gas lines can be seen in the parking strips.   The developer was also concerned that automobile parking would detract from sales so prohibitions on the number and location on the lot where cars could be parked were instituted.  A frustrated wealthy car collector built a 'spite house' on Forest Ave. just outside of the subdivision gates that features a large round-table on the first floor with chauffeur lodging above.

Sometime in the 1920's a Monkey tree was planted on the park.  Over the decades it grew to be very large.  During the 1960's, neighborhood children would meet at the tree in the evening to play tag and hide & seek.  The tree was 'base' for the games and eventually a large smooth spot developed on the tree from so many small hands clinging to it's safety.     Eventually, the Monkey tree grew so large that the City decided it was a potential hazard and removed it, but the name remained.

Although many believe it to be a 'dog park', it is not.  The park is reserved for cats on Tuesday and Thursday.

Great local gathering space for kids, dogs, neighbors.  Don't known where the name came from as I have visited the park for decade's & have never seen a monkey.  A permanent picnic table would be a nice addition.

top_reviews.content: An unmatched experience spending the evening at Paname and also being able to go back and forth to Paris right next door. The vibes are so good, welcoming and safe and the coolest folks work here. I love this space and will always choose this club first ☺️

I 100% recommend it! 🤩

Paname in San Francisco is a real favorite of mine! The atmosphere is incredible, the music is amazing, and the DJs keep the party going all night long 🔥 There’s such a festive vibe, with little nods to Paris in the décor. Having two rooms with two different vibes — especially with Paris 75 right next door — is also such a great bonus!

The themed nights are definitely a huge plus! Each event has its own universe, decor, and sometimes even a dress code, which makes the experience even more fun and immersive. It’s a refreshing change from repetitive nights out and makes you want to come back every time to discover the next theme.

The venue is well organized, the staff is friendly, and you feel safe.

The crowd is great, the energy is super positive, and you truly have a memorable night. If you’re looking for a place to dance, have fun, and enjoy an amazing night out in SF — this is the spot! 🥰

Great place! The music is always on point, and the bartenders are super friendly and professional. The cocktails are excellent, and there are so many different themed nights — you can never get bored!

I had my bday party here and got a table and also was the headlining DJ on a Friday night.  Mags, the talent buyer was amazing.  She was easy to work with and super accommodating.  Mags and the venue's hospitality were unmatched.  The venue provided the visuals and they were so awesome with all the correct logos for the DJs.  The bottle service girl came by often to make sure we had everything we needed.  The GM, Dolly, came by multiple times to check in making sure we were having a great time and that I had everything I needed as the DJ.  The venue is long and narrow but I never felt cramped with all my guests there and I had a lot of them.  The sound quality was great, loud but not too loud.  Mags came by multiple times to fill the room was smoke/filled bubbles!  Guests loved popping them.  There were lasers and sparklers...really felt like we were in Vegas.  There were other groups celebrating bdays and bachelorette party and honestly, it was a great night!  I would definitely come back to DJ or throw another party at Paname!

Paris meets Vegas in North Beach!

Right next door to Paris 75 (which I highly recommend checking out as well!), Paname is a brand new nightclub that brings a fresh, exciting energy to the heart of North Beach. The Parisian theme continues here too — the decor instantly reminds you of a stylish club in Paris, but the vibe? Definitely Vegas-level.

From the moment you walk in, the lights, the music, the crowd — it’s all electric. The space is big, clean, and super well-designed. What really stood out to me is how affordable the drinks are. Seriously, that’s pretty rare for San Francisco!

The bartenders are on point — friendly, fast, and super attentive. No waiting forever to get a drink, which is honestly a game-changer on a night out.

The music? Absolute fire. Great mixes, good energy, people dancing non-stop. And since it’s connected directly to Paris 75 from the inside, you can easily switch from chill cocktail bar to full nightclub mode — all in the same night.

Also, shoutout to Liam, the French owner, who’s created such a cool, welcoming space. The attention to detail is clear — even the bathrooms are clean, spacious, and well-maintained (you know that’s rare in clubs).

If you’re looking for a fun night out with French flair, great music, and fair prices, Paname is your new go-to.

The breakfast menu is impressive, with pastries like croissants, danishes, muffins, and banana bread, along with a variety of quiches and breakfast sandwiches. Options range from classic bacon, egg, and cheese to turkey or sausage sandwiches, and everything is clearly listed with fair prices. It’s easy to find something tasty, whether craving something light or a filling start to the morning.

Staff members like Oscar, Luis, and Aritri contribute a lot to the positive vibe. They are friendly and efficient, making every customer feel valued and at home. Service is quick and cheerful, making it an ideal stop for people on the go, but also relaxed enough that lingering over a drink and snack never feels rushed.

The pastry case is a real temptation, with beautifully presented treats like cheesecakes topped with bright cherries and chocolate shavings. Everything on display looks fresh and inviting, adding a sweet touch to the overall experience.

Overall, this spot offers a comfortable and inviting experience thanks to its creative décor, excellent staff, and wide selection of great breakfast items and desserts. It is dependable, welcoming, and well worth repeat visits for anyone looking for a good place to start the day or enjoy a relaxing coffee break.

I was particularly captivated by unique artifacts such as Acid Test recordings. Beyond the exhibits, the museum store offers a wonderful array of books. I wholeheartedly encourage everyone to experience this place; it's an invaluable opportunity to connect with the legacy of counterculture and truly grasp its profound relevance in our current times.

This new museum in the Haight-Ashbury neighborhood features many rare and original documents of the mid-1960s counterculture movement that sparked in the neighborhood. address: 446 Valencia St, San Francisco, CA 94103, United States

google.name: Eclectic Box SF
google.address: 446 Valencia St, San Francisco, CA 94103, United States

top_reviews.content:
It saddens me to write this review, because I was genuinely excited to support this small theatre company. I love intimate productions and was looking forward to an engaging night of live theatre — but what I witnessed left me feeling shaken and deeply disappointed.

My girlfriend and I went to see Coriolanus and purposely sat a few rows back, avoiding the designated audience participation seats. That choice ended up giving us a full view of an incident I wish I hadn’t witnessed.

At the start, the host encouraged us to cheer and engage with the show, assuring us the actors could handle it. The production clearly invited the audience to take a stance — rooting for “the people” and against the political figure Coriolanus, who was styled in a way that seemed meant to provoke (see the photo attached). Flyers were handed out to the front rows, and some audience members gently tossed their balled-up flyers toward the actor portraying Coriolanus, seemingly as part of the interactive experience. A total of probably 6 people on both sides of the rows participated in tossing the fliers.

It all felt in line with the tone that had been set — until it suddenly wasn’t. A staff member with purple hair, who had earlier welcomed us at the door, came storming down the aisle in a blind rage and screamed at the audience: “You will not throw paper at the actors!” She directed this specifically at one side of the audience — including a child who had tossed a flyer while sitting between his parents. Then she turned and stormed back up the stairs.

Moments later, the host returned with matching anger, warning the audience that anyone throwing papers would be asked to leave. The entire mood in the room shifted. People around me looked stunned, even disturbed. And I was too.

As someone with a history of trauma, witnessing a child being publicly yelled at like that was incredibly triggering. It didn’t need to be handled that way. A quiet word to the parents, a humorous note to the audience, even a gentle reminder from the host — there were so many better ways to address the situation without humiliation or rage.

It was heartbreaking. Not just for me, but for everyone around me who suddenly felt unwelcome in a space that should have been about connection, art, and community. The actors — especially the more seasoned performers — were excellent, but after that moment, it was hard to stay present in the story.

When the host returned at the end to thank us and ask for donations, it felt jarring. After being scolded so harshly, the thank-you felt hollow. I still believe in the potential of this company, but I hope they seriously reflect on how they treat their audiences — especially children. Theatre can challenge us, move us, provoke us — but it should never make us feel unsafe.

Lastly their website promotes that, “We strive to create opportunities for marginalized theatre-makers in the San Francisco Bay Area.” Which is wild to see an entirely visibly white cast with the exception of one black woman who was clearly a higher caliber actress. For a city as diverse as San Francisco this is a bit off putting and leaves me wondering why they don’t have a more culturally diverse cast. However if this is how the management treats the audience, it may add to the picture of why marginalized people may not want to work there.

top_reviews.content:
Tried the Afternoon Tea at Nudi Blue.
Beautiful presentation served in a glass case, everything felt like a little piece of art.
Great balance of sweet and savory. The blueberry peach scone was soft and fragrant and the tea sandwiches were light and well done. Desserts were refreshing and not too sweet.
Loved the rose and peach teas very aromatic, smooth and delicate.
Overall, a lovely afternoon tea experience. Perfect for relaxing or a cute photo moment.

Currently, afternoon tea is the primary offering at Nudi Blue. It includes a sweet course, a salad palate cleanser, a savory course, and two tea selections. You can purchase their impressive selection of teas and pastries à la carte, too.

The first course was a delightful selection of five pastries. The majority were croissant dough-based, but in different shapes and portion sizes. The guava croissant burst with tropical flavor, and its laminated layers had a good bounce. Pink guava cream decorated the top and filled the pastry.

I quite liked the Earl Grey NY Roll, which was a slice of croissant topped with earl grey cream. I do wish the candied tea leaves had a stronger flavor, but they looked lovely.

My favorite item was the half-moon croissant. The whipped dill cream cheese held its piped shape well. Artful bits of onion flakes and caviar were sprinkled and dolloped on top. That lovely cucumber ribbon and the dill fronds added nice flavor to each bite. I love all those flavors together, but I should note that I may also have loved the half-moon most because it was the most sizable item.

Both of the tartlets—pear and apple with lychee cream and a seasonal combination of citruses—were quite enjoyable, though messy to eat in a couple bites.

After I ate all my crumbs, I was happy to have a small, palate-cleansing salad served next. The vinaigrette was light and satisfying, and the simple mixed greens were boosted by thin shavings of strawberry, rhubarb, and leek.

And then it was time for the savory course, served on a fun glass case containing an artificial terrarium that evoked a creekside walk. I was less enchanted with this course overall. Honestly, I think that’s mostly because the milk bread used for the two sandwiches tasted stale and dry. The bread was toasted for the vibrantly arrayed smoked duck breast and blueberry sandwich, so that dryness was likely intentional. But as the duck itself was also on the dry side, it didn’t work for me. Also, I’m not a fan of blueberry and that is completely not Nudi Blue’s fault. I wanted to try that sandwich regardless, because it looked so inventive.

The cucumber sandwich included herbal cream cheese, a cucumber gelée, and a rauram leaf on top. Its milk bread was untoasted but still tasted dry and stale to me. It was also bigger than it needed to be? That’s odd to say for a tea sandwich, I know. Following my dining companion’s example, I found it more approachable to eat one layer at a time. It felt like too much cream cheese when taking a full bite. I couldn’t help but compare it with the half-moon croissant from the first course, and it didn’t wow like that one did.

The ham and quinta cheese bite, served on puff pastry, was a pleasant option. It went down fast, and I especially enjoyed the pomegranate seeds that added a burst of acidity to contrast with the richness of ham and cheese.

Much like the tartlets, I enjoyed both scones. The orange and jelly-topped scone had bold flavors but did not linger in my memory like the wagyu scone did. The latter wasn’t visually pleasing with just a slice of quinta cheese melted on top. And I was surprised by how few bits of ground wagyu were in the dough. But the richness of that scone was incredible! The texture was perfect, and I could taste the butter in the dough. I wonder if wagyu fat was also incorporated into it to make it taste that good. I would have easily eaten another, with or without the provided butter and honey.

Before the first course, we were given a tray of teas to sniff and decide on for our sweet and savory courses. Many of them are varieties of Thai tea leaves, which were new to me, though some English standards are also offered. Do note that some of the teas on offer are considered premium teas and cost a few dollars more, if you prefer them. As neither my friend nor I are tea connoisseurs, we did not opt for those and were satisfied with what we chose.

So did I enjoy the afternoon tea? Yes! The savory course has room for improvement, but the sweet course was pretty darn delicious the whole way through.

Absolutely fabulous afternoon tea! Friendly service, a cute backyard, delicious food (sweet and savory) and fresh tea. I love the concept and will be back. An extra plus — we are GF and they accommodated!

Super interesting teas with the giant tea being my favorite. First course was phenomenal. We went for the full tea service the third day it opened, and you can tell it’s only going to get better. Ambiance was great with a live piano player and handmade ceramic tea cups per person.

Loved it! Had to try Nudi Blue during its opening weekend, as I love, love, love their sister restaurant, Tanzies. Unlike any other high tea in the Bay Area. Attention to detail in every way, from stoneware to tea selections, to architecture and taste of every sandwich and pastry. Beautiful live piano music serenaded throughout. As with Tanzies, I was made to feel like I was a guest in their house, the service was so warm and welcoming. Will be back soon...

top_reviews.content:
Before I became too lazy, I used to go jogging a few times a week, and my route often took me past Brannan Street Wharf Park. Even now, it’s one of those small neighborhood spaces that quietly serves its purpose well. In the afternoons, it’s especially popular with local dog owners, office workers on breaks, and people simply looking for a place to sit, relax, and enjoy the water. While it’s not a large park, it is well-used and well-loved by the South Beach community.

What makes this spot particularly interesting is its history. This peaceful patch of green was once part of San Francisco’s gritty working waterfront, home to aging maritime structures including Pier 36. For decades, this stretch of the Embarcadero was dominated by heavy industry and shipping activity, until the old piers became too dilapidated to use safely. As part of the broader effort to revitalize the Embarcadero and reconnect the city with the Bay, the condemned pier and bulkhead wharf were demolished and transformed into public open space.

The park opened in 2013 and remains a cherished pocket of greenery built right over the water. It features a grassy lawn, picnic areas, a waterfront promenade, and distinctive tidal columns that display the changing bay water levels—a subtle nod to the area’s maritime roots. Today, it’s an excellent place to pause, people-watch, walk your dog, or simply take in the views of the Bay Bridge. It’s proof that even small parks can make a significant difference in a densely populated urban neighborhood.

Brannan Street Wharf Park is a small but really charming little spot. The grass area is perfect to lay a blanket, relax, or just take a quick break while walking by. The real highlight has to be the views—the Bay Bridge looks incredible from here, especially if you catch it during sunset or a clear day. It’s peaceful, not overcrowded, and just a really nice spot to soak in the waterfront vibes. Great for photos, a quick snack, or just enjoying a few quiet minutes outside in the city. Definitely one of those hidden gems that feels a little like your own personal slice of the Bay.

top_reviews.content:
I usually don’t write reviews, but I think this crepe store deserves more recognition! The location of this store is very good; it’s located at Park Street, which is incredibly accessible! The guy who took my order was very sweet and friendly! Service was very fast too! My order came out hot and fresh.

As for the taste of my order, I got a sweet crepe #7, Sweet Sunset, that included a very generous portion of strawberries and bananas. The taste of the strawberries and bananas were really refreshing, fresh, and sweet! Their ice cream selection is pretty good, offering matcha, cookies and cream, vanilla, strawberry and chocolate. I also really liked the texture of the crepe itself, it was slightly crispy yet bready combined with the Nutella makes the crepe come together to taste super rich.

As for the vibe of the store, the atmosphere is very clean, and has a lot of seats for customers. One thing I liked about the seats is that the owner put cushions for the marbled side which shows that they are really considerate for their customers. I also like the music they played it’s not too loud or too quiet, just the perfect volume. And I like how they have an LED backdrop to take picture of your order!

Basically this place deserves a 10/10, the portions again, were very generous but most importantly filling. I would definitely come back to order more with friends. Do give this spot a try!

Crepe Haven
⭐️⭐️ (2 stars)

I really wanted to love this place, because I genuinely love crepes—and I want local businesses to succeed.

Starting with the positives: we were greeted very warmly when we walked in, and that genuinely matters. Friendly staff alone earns a star in my book these days. The space itself is clean, cute, and comfortable, with seating that allows you to actually hear each other talk. It’s clearly geared toward a Gen Z crowd, which is totally fine, and they have a huge selection of sweet crepes—that seems to be their niche.

We ordered two savory crepes. They tasted fine, but for the price, the value just wasn’t there. Very simple fillings (tomato, lettuce, egg, a small amount of cheese), and we both walked away still feeling hungry. My husband’s reaction was that it felt low-quality—more like a nostalgic 90s lunchable or a basic DIY sandwich than something you’d go out for as a treat. For what we paid, we were hoping for something that felt more substantial or elevated than what we could easily make at home.

Service-wise, after ordering, we picked up our food ourselves and cleaned up after ourselves. With the current tip prompts, that felt a bit awkward—there wasn’t really table service or additional engagement beyond the initial friendliness, so the tipping expectation felt unclear.

We were walking by (didn’t park) and thought it would be fun to try somewhere new for a casual date-style treat. Unfortunately, we left feeling disappointed. I’ve had higher-quality crepes elsewhere for less, even accounting for rising prices right now.

Not a terrible experience—definitely not zero stars—but not one I’d rush back for, especially for savory crepes. If you’re really into sweet crepes and vibe with the aesthetic, this might be more your place. For us, it was a miss, and that’s a bummer.

Wow, I’m so glad we found this place!

It saved us though, because that ice cream will melt and drip from the bottom of the crepe cone.

TL;DR: If you enjoy escape rooms, skip this one.

I went to this escape room with a large group (10+) and it was a huge disappointment. I’ve done many escape rooms before, so I’m very familiar with how they’re supposed to work. This experience was nothing like that.

First, you are not placed in a private room with your group. Instead, multiple groups are packed into the same large space, and your “escape room” is just a small assigned corner. You spend a good portion of the game figuring out which props and clues actually belong to your group, while being surrounded by strangers who are also trying to play their own games. It completely breaks immersion and makes the experience frustrating rather than fun.

Despite staff insisting that groups are independent, that’s simply not true. You’re all sharing the same space, noise, and distractions, and the final section actually requires every group to solve their puzzles before anyone can finish. That means you’re forced to wait on strangers anyway.

The room itself was also in poor condition. Props were worn or falling apart, and some clues were handwritten in pencil and badly smudged. It felt sloppy and low-effort compared to even average escape rooms.

To make matters worse, the game masters repeatedly gave us solutions without us asking. It was obvious they were rushing us through because another group was queued up behind us. The whole experience felt like being herded through as quickly as possible rather than being allowed to enjoy the puzzles.

I honestly felt bad bringing friends here for their first escape room experience. Between the lack of privacy, poor-quality setup, and constant rushing, this was not fun or engaging. I strongly recommend looking elsewhere if you want a real escape room experience.

Absolutely fantastic experience at The Simples and Room! My wife and I have done dozens of escape rooms across the country, and this one easily ranks among the best. The puzzles were incredibly creative, thoughtfully designed, and—most importantly—doable. We never felt stuck for the wrong reasons, and each solution gave that satisfying “aha!” moment.

A huge shoutout to Kent and Robert, our game masters, who were both professional and fun. They added to the experience without ever being intrusive. Their enthusiasm and attention to detail really stood out.

We can’t wait to come back and try the other rooms they offer. If you’re looking for an escape room that challenges you in the best ways, this is it!
